      "@type": "Question",
      "name": "1. Introduction",
      "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/storm-overflows-policy-and-guidance/storm-overflows-policy-and-guidance#introduction",
      "acceptedAnswer": {
        "@type": "Answer",
        "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/storm-overflows-policy-and-guidance/storm-overflows-policy-and-guidance#introduction",
        "text": "\u003ch3 id=\"objectives\"\u003e1.1 Objectives\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe objectives of this publication are to provide advice to the sector on the management and regulation of storm overflows, including:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ereflecting the evolution in the understanding of storm overflows legislation and developments in policy since the \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1994/2841/contents\"\u003eUrban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations 1994\u003c/a\u003e (\u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994)\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eproviding additional information on how to implement measures identified in the \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/storm-overflows-discharge-reduction-plan\"\u003estorm overflows discharge reduction plan\u003c/a\u003e (\u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe intention is to support water and sewerage companies and the regulators in carrying out their responsibilities in relation to storm overflows.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e) wants to ensure a clear planning framework, to support:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe significant forward investment needed from water and sewerage companies\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ea robust oversight and enforcement regime\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eWe also want to ensure transparency and accountability, recognising the significant public interest in tackling sewage pollution, and to provide assurance to customers.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSince 1994, understanding of the legal requirements surrounding storm overflows has evolved. There have been updates to:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe interpretation of legal requirements, such as through the Court of Justice of the European Union in European Commission v UK (Re Storm Water Overflows) [2013] 1 CMLR 24\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003epolicy and regulatory tools that contribute to bringing these requirements into effect, for example via:\n    \u003cul\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003ethe Environment Agency (\u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e)’s storm overflow assessment framework (\u003cabbr title=\"storm overflow assessment framework\"\u003eSOAF\u003c/abbr\u003e) (first issued in 2018, updated in 2025)\u003c/li\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003ethe Environment Act 2021, which introduced requirements such as the need for the Secretary of State to prepare a \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e and for annual reports on discharges from storm overflows\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003c/ul\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eAlongside this, the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e, first published in 2022 and expanded in 2023, sets out an investment and improvement programme to 2050 with the aim of reducing harm to public health and the environment from storm overflows. The \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e contains 3 headline targets that water and sewerage companies will deliver over the next 25 years.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAs the legal and policy landscape has developed, so has technological capability. All storm overflows operated by water and sewerage companies whose areas are wholly or mainly in England are now fitted with event duration monitors (\u003cabbr title=\"event duration monitors\"\u003eEDMs\u003c/abbr\u003e), allowing water and sewerage companies to report on the frequency and duration of storm overflow discharges in near real time.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"event duration monitor\"\u003eEDM\u003c/abbr\u003e data provides greater insight into the operation of storm overflows than ever before. It should be utilised by water and sewerage companies and regulators to inform daily operation, maintenance of and required upgrades to the sewerage system.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eMonitoring data can also be used to help identify possible compliance issues with legal requirements. This publication seeks to provide greater clarity on how monitoring data may be used to inform investigations and storm overflow improvements.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOn 23 October 2024, the UK and Welsh governments launched an independent commission to recommend reforms to reset the water sector regulatory system. The commission aims to build consensus for a resilient and innovative water sector and a robust regulatory framework that will:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edeliver long-term benefits\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003erestore rivers, lakes and seas to good health\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eprovide a reliable and efficient water supply in a changing climate\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eultimately, serve both customers and the environment\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eOnce the commission has made recommendations, both governments will respond and consult on proposals, including potential legislation.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"scope-and-how-we-expect-this-publication-to-be-used\"\u003e1.2 Scope and how we expect this publication to be used\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis publication is intended to provide information and strategic guidance for the management and regulation of storm overflows, from the point of assessment to the delivery of improvements and enforcement of regulatory requirements.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis document does not impose any new legal requirements on regulators or water and sewerage companies. It is instead restating and clarifying the current position on storm overflows regulation and management, including to support preparations for future price reviews.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"scope\"\u003e1.2.1 Scope\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis publication applies to water and sewerage companies and regulators in respect of storm overflows operated by water and sewerage companies whose area is wholly or mainly in England. In this context, ‘regulators’ refers to Ofwat or the Environment Agency (\u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e). \u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThere are approximately 14,500 storm overflows in England, both on the network and at wastewater treatment works. This publication also applies to storm overflows at pumping stations, which serve combined systems (both rainfall runoff and foul flow). They act as hydraulic control for flows in excess of the designed pump rate to treatment.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt does not apply to other types of assets or overflows including emergency overflows, due to the different applications of these assets and the different regulatory schemes which apply to these.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"areas-of-focus\"\u003e1.2.2 Areas of focus\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis document opens with a focus on advancements in relation to the monitoring of storm overflows, and how resultant data can be used to support the delivery of storm overflow improvements and compliance with legal and policy requirements.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt then provides a summary of the legislative and policy requirements for storm overflows, under the \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994 and the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e. It sets out how the ‘best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs’ (\u003cabbr title=\"best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs\"\u003eBTKNEEC\u003c/abbr\u003e) test should be implemented in practice, taking into account relevant case law and developments, and provides further detail on how the targets under the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e should be met.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eMoving onto implementation, the document explains how investigations should be carried out, and how improvements should be delivered. This section of the document seeks to provide advice for regulators in carrying out their statutory duties, as well as considerations for water and sewerage companies to support them in planning and delivering the substantial forward investment programme required.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe document then summarises \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e, the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e and Ofwat’s enforcement responsibilities.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFinally, this document updates elements of previous \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e guidance on storm overflows. Draft guidance on the \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994 was issued to dischargers and regulators in July 1997 (the 1997 guidance). It was intended as a working document for dischargers and regulators on the implementation and interpretation of the \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994. Information in respect of storm overflows was largely found in Annex 8 of the 1997 guidance, which covered:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe definition of unsatisfactory overflows\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003econsenting for satisfactory and unsatisfactory overflows\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe procedure for reviewing overflows to freshwaters and discharges into coastal waters and estuaries\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eWith the exception of a limited update in 2009, the 1997 guidance has not been revised since it was published. This document now supersedes parts of Annex 3 and all of Annex 8 for storm overflows operated by water and sewerage companies whose area is wholly or mainly in England (but not for storm overflows operated by water and sewerage companies whose area is wholly or mainly in Wales). Those parts of the 1997 guidance will be withdrawn and replaced by Section 7 of this document. The rest of the 1997 guidance is still applicable.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSection 7 has been provided by the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e and is intended as a guideline for water and sewerage companies. Companies should also refer to the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e’s latest guidance (including the storm overflow assessment framework (\u003cabbr title=\"storm overflow assessment framework\"\u003eSOAF\u003c/abbr\u003e) version 2) and relevant legal requirements.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis document signposts other technical and regulatory guidance where appropriate, such as the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e’s \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflow assessment framework\"\u003eSOAF\u003c/abbr\u003e version 2. The \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflow assessment framework\"\u003eSOAF\u003c/abbr\u003e version 2 sets out technical details and processes for prioritising the investigation and improvement of individual assets. It should be read in conjunction with:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe requirement to provide and maintain the sewerage network under section 94 of the Water Industry Act 1991 (\u003cabbr title=\"Water Industry Act 1991\"\u003eWIA 1991\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"how-this-publication-should-be-used\"\u003e1.2.3 How this publication should be used\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis publication is non-statutory and is not intended to replace or amend existing legislative requirements. In addition, while every effort has been made to ensure that explanations included in this document are accurate, only the courts can give authoritative interpretation of the law.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThere may also be legal obligations to which this document does not refer, but which must be complied with. Water and sewerage companies should seek legal advice and consult with regulators where they are unclear about the scope and effect of applicable legislation.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt is ultimately water and sewerage companies’ responsibility to ensure that they comply with their legal requirements.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis publication will be kept under review and updated as needed, including in advance of \u003cabbr title=\"2029 price review\"\u003ePR29\u003c/abbr\u003e (2030 to 2035).\u003c/p\u003e"
      }
    },

      "@type": "Question",
      "name": "2. Monitoring and advancements in data",
      "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/storm-overflows-policy-and-guidance/storm-overflows-policy-and-guidance#monitoring-and-advancements-in-data",
      "acceptedAnswer": {
        "@type": "Answer",
        "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/storm-overflows-policy-and-guidance/storm-overflows-policy-and-guidance#monitoring-and-advancements-in-data",
        "text": "\u003cp\u003eThis section reflects key developments in monitoring and data since the \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994. It does not provide an exhaustive list of storm overflow monitoring requirements.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"event-duration-monitoring\"\u003e2.1 Event duration monitoring\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eAll storm overflows now have monitors installed recording the frequency and duration of their operation. The programme to install event duration monitors (\u003cabbr title=\"event duration monitors\"\u003eEDMs\u003c/abbr\u003e) on storm overflows was completed in December 2023.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e will continue to oversee \u003cabbr title=\"event duration monitor\"\u003eEDM\u003c/abbr\u003e installation, operation and reporting by way of their functions under the Environmental Permitting (England and Wales) Regulations 2016 (the \u003cabbr title=\"Environmental Permitting (England and Wales) Regulations 2016\"\u003eEPR 2016\u003c/abbr\u003e).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWater and sewerage companies should refer to industry best practice on \u003cabbr title=\"event duration monitors\"\u003eEDMs\u003c/abbr\u003e. This includes the Chartered Institution of Water and Environmental Management (\u003cabbr title=\"Chartered Institution of Water and Environmental Management\"\u003eCIWEM\u003c/abbr\u003e) \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.ciwem.org/assets/uploads/CIWEM_UDG_EDM_Good_Practice_Guide_2021_final.pdf\"\u003eEvent Duration Monitoring Good Practice Guide\u003c/a\u003e. They should ensure that monitors are appropriately accredited and perform in line with \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e and Ofwat guidance.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"annual-edm-reporting\"\u003e2.1.1 Annual \u003cabbr title=\"event duration monitor\"\u003eEDM\u003c/abbr\u003e reporting\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e has a duty under section 141D of the \u003cabbr title=\"Water Industry Act 1991\"\u003eWIA 1991\u003c/abbr\u003e (inserted by the Environment Act 2021) to publish an annual summary of measured \u003cabbr title=\"event duration monitor\"\u003eEDM\u003c/abbr\u003e data by the end of March each year for the preceding calendar year.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWater and sewerage companies should present \u003cabbr title=\"event duration monitor\"\u003eEDM\u003c/abbr\u003e data for annual reporting and compliance purposes using the 12 hour and 24 hour block spill counting method, as described in section 3.2 of this document. Information from \u003cabbr title=\"event duration monitors\"\u003eEDMs\u003c/abbr\u003e regarding start and stop times of a discharge should be maintained by water and sewerage companies and made available to regulators on request.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor storm overflows determined as having potential to impact on designated bathing waters, water and sewerage companies should provide a report to the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e on \u003cabbr title=\"event duration monitor\"\u003eEDM\u003c/abbr\u003e and storm overflow performance for the period of the bathing season (May to September).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"near-real-time-reporting-of-edm-data\"\u003e2.1.2 Near real time reporting of \u003cabbr title=\"event duration monitor\"\u003eEDM\u003c/abbr\u003e data\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eSince 1 January 2025, water and sewerage companies have been required to publish storm overflow data in near real time, pursuant to the requirement introduced by section 81 of the Environment Act 2021.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThat section introduced a duty for water and sewerage companies to publish information on when a storm overflow discharge:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ebegins and the location of the storm overflow (within an hour of the discharge beginning)\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eends (within an hour of the discharge ending)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis information should be published in a way which is readily accessible and understandable to the public.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOfwat, is responsible for overseeing compliance with this duty. Ofwat’s 2024 price review (\u003cabbr title=\"2024 price review\"\u003ePR24\u003c/abbr\u003e) \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.ofwat.gov.uk/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/Storm-overflows-PC-definition.pdf\"\u003ecommon performance commitments for storm overflows\u003c/a\u003e will incentivise water and sewerage companies to maintain \u003cabbr title=\"event duration monitors\"\u003eEDMs\u003c/abbr\u003e and record discharges. The performance measure calculation takes monitored spills and unmonitored storm overflows into consideration.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"use-of-edm-data-for-regulatory-purposes\"\u003e2.1.3 Use of \u003cabbr title=\"event duration monitor\"\u003eEDM\u003c/abbr\u003e data for regulatory purposes\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e will use \u003cabbr title=\"event duration monitor\"\u003eEDM\u003c/abbr\u003e data to:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003einform their duties in the regulation of storm overflows\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eassess delivery against targets, including those laid out in the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eOfwat will utilise \u003cabbr title=\"event duration monitor\"\u003eEDM\u003c/abbr\u003e data to inform their:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eenforcement duties in the regulation of storm overflows\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003epolicy and decisions in relation to water and sewerage companies’ investment programmes, to ensure their sewerage assets are and continue to be built and operated to meet their environmental obligations\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e and Ofwat will continue to review any technological advancements in monitoring. Where appropriate, advancements may inform specific \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e permit conditions, which may result in enhanced obligations for water and sewerage companies to implement additional data monitoring requirements. Examples of possible advancements include:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003enew monitoring intervals\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ereporting frequencies\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003erequirements for telemetry\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eassurance and certification schemes\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"continuous-water-quality-monitoring-of-the-receiving-water-environment\"\u003e2.2 Continuous water quality monitoring of the receiving water environment\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eWater and sewerage companies are beginning to install continuous water quality monitoring (\u003cabbr title=\"continuous water quality monitoring\"\u003eCWQM\u003c/abbr\u003e) monitors in the \u003cabbr title=\"2024 price review\"\u003ePR24\u003c/abbr\u003e period (2025 to 2030), focusing on high priority assets.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWater quality metrics measured by the \u003cabbr title=\"continuous water quality monitoring\"\u003eCWQM\u003c/abbr\u003e programme are specifically aligned to those required to assess receiving water quality against the urban pollution management (\u003cabbr title=\"urban pollution management\"\u003eUPM\u003c/abbr\u003e) fundamental intermittent standards (\u003cabbr title=\"fundamental intermittent standards\"\u003eFIS\u003c/abbr\u003e) for levels of ammonia, dissolved oxygen, temperatures, pH values and turbidity.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eData collected in accordance with the \u003cabbr title=\"continuous water quality monitoring\"\u003eCWQM\u003c/abbr\u003e programme will be used by regulators and water and sewerage companies to inform the development of schemes to deliver the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e requirements, particularly the ecological target (see section 3.2).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe data will also support:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe successful delivery of improvement schemes to meet storm overflow legal requirements and targets\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e river basin planning work in assessing reasons for not achieving good status (\u003cabbr title=\"reasons for not achieving good status\"\u003eRNAGS\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe regulators will also use this data alongside \u003cabbr title=\"event duration monitor\"\u003eEDM\u003c/abbr\u003e data to inform their policy and enforcement activities, for example to check for permit breaches.\u003c/p\u003e"
      }
    },
    {
      "@type": "Question",
      "name": "3. Basis for storm overflow improvements",
      "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/storm-overflows-policy-and-guidance/storm-overflows-policy-and-guidance#basis-for-storm-overflow-improvements",
      "acceptedAnswer": {
        "@type": "Answer",
        "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/storm-overflows-policy-and-guidance/storm-overflows-policy-and-guidance#basis-for-storm-overflow-improvements",
        "text": "\u003ch3 id=\"legal-requirements\"\u003e3.1 Legal requirements\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis section outlines key legal requirements that apply to the use and maintenance of storm overflows, and to associated enforcement action.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOf central importance here are the Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations 1994 (‘\u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e’), which include (among other things) requirements for the design and operation of sewers, treatment works and storm overflows, whilst also setting out the treatment standards to be applied.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis section should not be treated as an exhaustive list of the applicable legal requirements in this area, and water and sewerage companies should continue to refer to relevant legislation and case law. Regulators can also be consulted for advice.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"statutory-requirements\"\u003e3.1.1 Statutory requirements\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eSection 94 of the Water Industry Act 1991 (\u003cabbr title=\"Water Industry Act 1991\"\u003eWIA 1991\u003c/abbr\u003e) imposes a duty on water and sewerage companies to provide, improve and extend such a system of public sewers, and so to cleanse and maintain those sewers, as to ensure that the area is and continues to be effectually drained.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eCompanies are also required to make provision for the emptying of those sewers and such further provision as is necessary from time to time for effectually dealing with (by means of sewage disposal or otherwise) the contents of those sewers.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994 transposed the Urban Waste Water Treatment Directive (the \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment Directive\"\u003eUWWTD\u003c/abbr\u003e) with respect to England and Wales. They supplement section 94 of the \u003cabbr title=\"Water Industry Act 1991\"\u003eWIA 1991\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eTogether, the \u003cabbr title=\"Water Industry Act 1991\"\u003eWIA 1991\u003c/abbr\u003e and the \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994 impose obligations on water and sewerage companies, the Secretary of State, and regulators. In this context, ‘regulators’ refers to Ofwat, and the applicable of the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e or Natural Resources Wales.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhere obligations are not complied with, regulators can take enforcement action, relying on powers conferred under the \u003cabbr title=\"Water Industry Act 1991\"\u003eWIA 1991\u003c/abbr\u003e or the \u003cabbr title=\"Environmental Permitting (England and Wales) Regulations 2016\"\u003eEPR 2016\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"duties-on-water-and-sewerage-companies\"\u003e3.1.2 Duties on water and sewerage companies\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eRegulation 4 of the \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994 sets out mandatory requirements for water and sewerage companies when carrying out their duties to provide and maintain adequate sewerage systems under section 94 of the \u003cabbr title=\"Water Industry Act 1991\"\u003eWIA 1991\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRegulation 4 contains obligations in respect of both collecting systems and treatment plants. Key obligations include that companies must:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1. Ensure collecting systems meet the requirements set out in Schedule 2 (regulation 4(2)). Paragraph 2 of Schedule 2 provides that collecting systems should be designed, constructed and maintained in accordance with the ‘best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs’ (\u003cabbr title=\"best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs\"\u003eBTKNEEC\u003c/abbr\u003e) test, particularly in relation to the:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003evolume and characteristics of urban waste water\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eprevention of leaks\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003elimitation of pollution of receiving waters due to storm water overflows\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eTo note, the Court of Justice of the European Union (\u003cabbr title=\"Court of Justice of the European Union\"\u003eCJEU\u003c/abbr\u003e) clarified at [63] of European Commission v UK (Re Storm Water Overflows) [2013] 1 CMLR 24 that the \u003cabbr title=\"best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs\"\u003eBTKNEEC\u003c/abbr\u003e test extends to treatment plants as well as collecting systems.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2. Ensure that treatment plants are designed (account being taken of seasonal variations of the load), constructed, operated and maintained, to ensure sufficient performance under all normal local climatic conditions (regulation 4(4)(a)).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3. Ensure disposal routes for treated waste water and sludge minimise adverse effects on the environment (regulation 4(4)(c)).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe term collecting system refers to a system of sewers for collecting and conducting urban waste water.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eCompanies are responsible for ensuring compliance with the relevant legal requirements. Where necessary, companies should liaise with regulators regarding any questions they may have on requirements related to specific assets or permit conditions. This includes liaising with the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e to ensure assets and permits remain compliant with the obligations under the \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e. Companies must comply with permit conditions and ensure that all details contained on the permit are accurate.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"duties-on-regulators\"\u003e3.1.3 Duties on regulators\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eRegulation 6 of the \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994 imposes a duty on the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e when exercising their functions under the \u003cabbr title=\"Environmental Permitting (England and Wales) Regulations 2016\"\u003eEPR 2016\u003c/abbr\u003e (such as in granting, varying or revoking environmental permits), to secure ‘the limitation of pollution of receiving waters due to storm overflows’ in respect of discharges from collecting systems and treatment plants (regulation 6(2)(c)).\u003csup id=\"fnref:1\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:1\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 1]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e should review and, where appropriate, vary permit conditions in such a way as to reflect \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e and other legislative requirements (see relevant \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e permitting guidance).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOfwat also has responsibility for enforcing regulation 4 \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994, as it supplements the duty in section 94 \u003cabbr title=\"Water Industry Act 1991\"\u003eWIA 1991\u003c/abbr\u003e which Ofwat also enforces.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"case-law-and-the-btkneec-test\"\u003e3.1.4 Case law and the \u003cabbr title=\"best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs\"\u003eBTKNEEC\u003c/abbr\u003e test\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe requirements under the \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994 were considered by the Court of Justice of the European Union (\u003cabbr title=\"Court of Justice of the European Union\"\u003eCJEU\u003c/abbr\u003e) in European Commission v UK (Re Storm Water Overflows) [2013] 1 CMLR 24. The \u003cabbr title=\"Court of Justice of the European Union\"\u003eCJEU\u003c/abbr\u003e’s findings were summarised by the High Court at [63]-[70] of R (on the application of WildFish Conservation and Marine Conservation Society and others) v Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (‘WildFish’) [2023] EHWC 2285 (Admin).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Court of Justice of the European Union\"\u003eCJEU\u003c/abbr\u003e identified that:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eall urban waste water must be collected and treated under usual climatic and seasonal conditions\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ea failure to treat urban waste water can only be tolerated where the circumstances are ‘out of the ordinary’\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eAt the same time, the \u003cabbr title=\"Court of Justice of the European Union\"\u003eCJEU\u003c/abbr\u003e acknowledged footnote 1 to Annexes 1(A) and 1(B) of the \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment Directive\"\u003eUWWTD\u003c/abbr\u003e, which recognises that it is not possible in practice to construct collecting systems and treatment plants so that all waste water is capable of being treated. Such situations can be tolerated in “situations such as unusually heavy rainfall”, which the \u003cabbr title=\"Court of Justice of the European Union\"\u003eCJEU\u003c/abbr\u003e characterised as “exceptional situations” or “exceptional circumstances”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eHowever, in those situations the state must decide on “measures to limit pollution from storm water overflows”. As per the \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment Directive\"\u003eUWWTD\u003c/abbr\u003e footnote, such measures could be based on dilution rates or capacity in relation to dry weather flow, or could specify a certain acceptable number of overflows per year.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn practice, this means that discharges of untreated waste water from collecting systems and treatment plants should only occur in exceptional circumstances, unless remedial intervention would not satisfy the \u003cabbr title=\"best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs\"\u003eBTKNEEC\u003c/abbr\u003e test.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ePer the summary of the \u003cabbr title=\"Court of Justice of the European Union\"\u003eCJEU\u003c/abbr\u003e’s findings in WildFish, the \u003cabbr title=\"best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs\"\u003eBTKNEEC\u003c/abbr\u003e test involves weighing the best technology and its estimated costs against the benefits, or avoidance of harm, that a more effective water collection or treatment system may provide.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis involves taking into account the effects of discharges of untreated waste on the environment to see whether the costs that must be incurred or the works necessary to treat all waste water, would be proportionate to the environmental benefit that would result.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eStorm overflow discharges should therefore be assessed via the following two-stage test:\u003c/p\u003e\u003col\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eIs the storm overflow discharging outside of ‘exceptional circumstances’?\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eIf the discharge is not due to exceptional circumstances, is there a solution to improve the storm overflow which satisfies the \u003cabbr title=\"best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs\"\u003eBTKNEEC\u003c/abbr\u003e test?\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe two-stage test should be applied on a case-by-case basis.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRegulators and water and sewerage companies are expected to have regard to any relevant updates in case law on storm overflows when exercising their legal obligations.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"implementation-of-the-two-stage-test\"\u003e3.1.5 Implementation of the two-stage test\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e’s \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflow assessment framework\"\u003eSOAF\u003c/abbr\u003e version 2 (when published), and \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.water.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/Storm-Overflow-Benefits-Vaulation-Final-Practitioners-Guide.pdf\"\u003eguidance on valuing the benefits of storm discharge improvements\u003c/a\u003e (\u003cabbr title=\"cost-benefit analysis\"\u003eCBA\u003c/abbr\u003e process and Practitioners’ Guide are subject to review ahead of updating in 2025) provide a framework to support water and sewerage companies in identifying storm overflows which need remediation. This includes setting out guidance for how companies should carry out the \u003cabbr title=\"best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs\"\u003eBTKNEEC\u003c/abbr\u003e test.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e expects the two-stage test to be applied in a robust and consistent manner across all storm overflows and water and sewerage companies.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRegulators will set an appropriate benefit cost ratio (\u003cabbr title=\"benefit cost ratio\"\u003eBCR\u003c/abbr\u003e) to determine excessive cost. The \u003cabbr title=\"benefit cost ratio\"\u003eBCR\u003c/abbr\u003e will be set and updated according to best practice and best available evidence.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWater and sewerage companies must report to the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e after both stages of the two-stage test and provide all \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflow assessment framework\"\u003eSOAF\u003c/abbr\u003e outcomes to the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e, including where there is no solution which satisfies the \u003cabbr title=\"best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs\"\u003eBTKNEEC\u003c/abbr\u003e test, as outlined in the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflow assessment framework\"\u003eSOAF\u003c/abbr\u003e version 2.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn practice, water and sewerage companies provide this information to the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e via their annual \u003cabbr title=\"event duration monitor\"\u003eEDM\u003c/abbr\u003e returns. The \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e verifies this information and makes it available to Ofwat alongside its publication.    \u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e will develop a specific reporting mechanism for more frequent updates on the progress of \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflow assessment framework\"\u003eSOAF\u003c/abbr\u003e investigations and improvements. They will share this data as appropriate with other regulators.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWater and sewerage companies should keep their \u003cabbr title=\"best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs\"\u003eBTKNEEC\u003c/abbr\u003e assessments up to date and review them periodically, at least every 5 years. The depth of a review will generally depend on what has changed since the previous assessment and should be determined by water and sewerage companies on a case-by-case basis. Factors that may highlight the need for a review, and will help determine the scope of a review, include:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003echange in spill frequency or duration\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eadditional designations (such as a new bathing water site)\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eother changes in the catchment\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003erisk or change identified in the drainage and wastewater management plan (\u003cabbr title=\"drainage and wastewater management plan\"\u003eDWMP\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003enew technology is available\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003enew information on benefits or costs\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eKeeping \u003cabbr title=\"best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs\"\u003eBTKNEEC\u003c/abbr\u003e tests up to date should ensure that:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe design, build, operation and maintenance of each asset remains consistent with \u003cabbr title=\"best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs\"\u003eBTKNEEC\u003c/abbr\u003e as knowledge develops\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe changing costs and benefits at each site are reflected as they evolve\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe network is maintained, improved and extended as needed\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"unusually-heavy-rainfall-events\"\u003e3.1.6 Unusually heavy rainfall events\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eAs set out above, ‘unusually heavy rainfall’ was characterised as an ‘exceptional circumstance’ by the \u003cabbr title=\"Court of Justice of the European Union\"\u003eCJEU\u003c/abbr\u003e in the ‘UK’ case. The \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflow assessment framework\"\u003eSOAF\u003c/abbr\u003e version 2 sets out a methodology for identifying ‘unusually heavy’ rainfall events for the purpose of prioritising investigations to assets which spill frequently in more typical years.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"policy--storm-overflows-discharge-reduction-plan\"\u003e3.2 Policy – storm overflows discharge reduction plan\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis section provides further information on the implementation of the targets contained in the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e. It does not add to the requirements on water and sewerage companies outlined in the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e but provides additional guidance on delivery against the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e’s targets.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e, published in accordance with section 141A of the \u003cabbr title=\"Water Industry Act 1991\"\u003eWIA 1991\u003c/abbr\u003e, set 3 ambitious targets for water and sewerage companies:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ean ecological target and public health target (with these being the main drivers for improvement)\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ea rainfall target (interpreted as a maximum of 10 recorded spills on average per year as reported in the statutory \u003cabbr title=\"event duration monitor\"\u003eEDM\u003c/abbr\u003e return)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe targets in the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e were augmented by the 2023 update to the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e, which included a greater spread of high priority sites. High priority sites are defined in the ‘Ecological target’ sub-section (3.2.2).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e aims to increase ambition on reducing the harm caused by storm overflows. It goes further than the \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994 in most circumstances because improvements to meet its targets are not subject to a cost-benefit style assessment.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhile the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e has a statutory basis by virtue of its being required by the amendments made to the \u003cabbr title=\"Water Industry Act 1991\"\u003eWIA 1991\u003c/abbr\u003e by the Environment Act 2021, the contents of the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e are not legally binding. Water and sewerage companies have, however, committed to delivering against these targets. Compliance with the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e targets at an asset level will be implemented by way of environmental permits.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAn update on delivery against the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e targets will be published in \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e’s 2025 progress report, as required by the Environment Act 2021.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"implementation-of-the-targets\"\u003e3.2.1 Implementation of the targets\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eWater and sewerage companies should use the technologies, data and modelling available to them to ensure their sewer networks are operated to meet their legal obligations and the targets set out in the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e. Considerations that apply to particular \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e targets are outlined in sections 3.2.2 to 3.2.4.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThere are also some general considerations applicable to achievement of all of the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e targets, which are detailed in this section.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThese considerations have been developed in conjunction with the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e, as the expert organisation responsible for the regulatory implementation of the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"length-of-period-to-assess-average-spill-performance\"\u003e3.2.1.1 Length of period to assess average spill performance\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e spill frequency targets for storm overflows (ecological, bathing and rainfall targets) are defined as an average over 10 consecutive years.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt is recognised that a 10-year assessment requires significant time to determine permit compliance and therefore, to secure early identification of underperforming storm overflows, the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e may use a shorter-term regulatory compliance assessment.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"spill-counting-methodology\"\u003e3.2.1.2 Spill counting methodology\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThere is a distinction between ‘discharges’ and ‘spills’.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhen a signal from an \u003cabbr title=\"event duration monitor\"\u003eEDM\u003c/abbr\u003e device is verified, this means that a storm overflow discharge has taken place. For the purposes of \u003cabbr title=\"event duration monitor\"\u003eEDM\u003c/abbr\u003e on storm overflows that discharge to the environment, spills (or spill count) is the discharge count with the 12 and 24 hour block spill counting methodology applied.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFurther detail on how this counting methodology works in practice, including when assessing against spill targets, can be found in the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e’s \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflow assessment framework\"\u003eSOAF\u003c/abbr\u003e version 2.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"counting-and-discounting-spills\"\u003e3.2.1.2 Counting and discounting spills\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhen assessing against spill targets, the 12 and 24 hour block spill count of the individual assets should be assessed in isolation against the applicable \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e target. Spills from multiple discharges into a common receiving water should not be aggregated together when assessing against a spill count threshold. \u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf assessing against an ecological or environmental quality standard in the receiving waters, such as a shellfish water, then the combined effects of multiple storm overflows will be assessed.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eNo discharges or ‘calculated spills’ (which are spills counted using the 12 and 24 hour block spill count method) shall be discounted or removed from the counting process or spill count on the basis of small volume being considered likely to have no or small impact on the receiving waters.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"design-horizons-for-improvement-schemes\"\u003e3.2.1.3 Design horizons for improvement schemes\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhen designing spill performance against a spill target, it is recommended that a rainfall series of up to 25 years is used, due to the annual variability of rainfall.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRecognising that this will not always be possible, a minimum of 10 years’ data should be assessed.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf insufficient historical rainfall is available, a synthetic rainfall series will need to be developed. \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.ciwem.org/assets/pdf/Special%20Interest%20Groups/Urban%20Drainage%20Group/CIWEM-UDG-Rainfall-Guide-2016.pdf\"\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Chartered Institution of Water and Environmental Management\"\u003eCIWEM\u003c/abbr\u003e Rainfall Modelling Guide\u003c/a\u003e should be followed.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe rainfall series should be typical over the duration of the series and wet or exceptionally wet years should not be removed.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"using-sewer-hydraulic-models-to-design-against-spill-targets\"\u003e3.2.1.4 Using sewer hydraulic models to design against spill targets\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eStorm overflow improvements to meet spill frequency targets should make use of sewer hydraulic modelling.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eModels should be built, verified, applied and maintained in accordance with the \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.ciwem.org/assets/pdf/Special%20Interest%20Groups/Urban%20Drainage%20Group/Code%20of%20Practice%20for%20the%20Hydraulic%20Modelling%20of%20Ur.pdf\"\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Chartered Institution of Water and Environmental Management\"\u003eCIWEM\u003c/abbr\u003e Code of Practice for the Hydraulic Modelling of Urban Drainage Systems\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"strategic-planning-and-allowing-for-climate-change-and-other-pressures-on-sewerage-in-the-design\"\u003e3.2.1.5 Strategic planning and allowing for climate change and other pressures on sewerage in the design\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eCapacity pressures on sewerage systems include climate change (rainfall), population growth and urban creep, as well as ageing assets.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWater and sewerage companies should design their storm overflow improvements using planning horizons over the longer term (to 25 years) to address complex environmental issues and account for a range of future climate change scenarios and other pressures. \u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt is the water and sewerage companies’ responsibility to achieve and maintain storm overflow performance against the spill frequency targets. Failure to do so could result in permit non-compliance.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWater and sewerage companies should manage the current and future risks to and demands of their drainage and sewerage systems through their \u003cabbr title=\"drainage and wastewater management plans\"\u003eDWMPs\u003c/abbr\u003e, updated every 5 years and reviewed every year. These plans are required under section 94A of the \u003cabbr title=\"Water Industry Act 1991\"\u003eWIA 1991\u003c/abbr\u003e (inserted by section 79 of the Environment Act 2021).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ePreparing, publishing and maintaining \u003cabbr title=\"drainage and wastewater management plans\"\u003eDWMPs\u003c/abbr\u003e became a statutory requirement for water and sewerage companies from September 2024. Companies are expected to publish \u003cabbr title=\"drainage and wastewater management plans\"\u003eDWMPs\u003c/abbr\u003e ahead of \u003cabbr title=\"2029 price review\"\u003ePR29\u003c/abbr\u003e, after which statutory annual reviews will commence.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"assessing-performance-against-the-average-spill-targets\"\u003e3.2.1.6 Assessing performance against the average spill targets\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhen assessing spill performance against design targets, the spill performance should be assessed as an average over 10 years. This ensures equivalence against the design target of using a minimum of 10 years’ rainfall to design the storm overflow performance.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"assessing-compliance\"\u003e3.2.1.7 Assessing compliance\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e will protect the spill performance of storm overflow improvement schemes, and the performance of storm overflows which already meet design targets, through spill limit conditions within permits issued under the \u003cabbr title=\"Environmental Permitting (England and Wales) Regulations 2016\"\u003eEPR 2016\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eNon-compliance with limits in permit conditions could result in water and sewerage company investigations and enforcement action.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"ecological-target\"\u003e3.2.2 Ecological target\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e sets out that water and sewerage companies will only be permitted to discharge from a storm overflow where they can demonstrate that there is no local adverse ecological impact, by the deadlines set out in section 3.2.2.1.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis target will ensure that no water body in England fails to achieve good ecological status due to storm overflow discharges. Good ecological status is described in the Water Framework Directive 2000/60/EC (\u003cabbr title=\"Water Framework Directive\"\u003eWFD\u003c/abbr\u003e), Annex V, 1.2, table 1.2, as follows:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e“The values of the biological quality elements for the surface water body type show low levels of distortion resulting from human activity, but deviate only slightly from those normally associated with the surface water body type under undisturbed conditions.”\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"timelines-for-the-ecological-target\"\u003e3.2.2.1 Timelines for the ecological target\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eWater and sewerage companies will only be permitted to discharge from a storm overflow where they can demonstrate that there is no adverse ecological impact by the following target dates:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e2035 for at least 75% of storm overflows discharging into or near ‘high priority sites’\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e2045 for all overflows discharging into or near ‘high priority sites’\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e2050 for all remaining storm overflows\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe timeframes for improvements are also dependent on the sensitivities of the receiving waters and any known impacts, such as to bathing waters and ecological ‘high priority sites’.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"definition-of-ecological-high-priority-sites\"\u003e3.2.2.2 Definition of ecological ‘high priority sites’\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e, ‘high priority sites’ are defined as:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003esites of special scientific interest (\u003cabbr title=\"sites of special scientific interest\"\u003eSSSIs\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003especial areas of conservation (\u003cabbr title=\"special areas of conservation\"\u003eSACs\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003especial protected areas (\u003cabbr title=\"special protection areas\"\u003eSPAs\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eRamsar sites – wetlands of international importance designated under the Ramsar Convention\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003echalk streams\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994 sensitive areas\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003emarine conservation zones (\u003cabbr title=\"marine conservation zones\"\u003eMCZs\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewaters currently failing ecological standards due to storm overflows\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eshellfish water protected areas\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"assessing-whether-a-storm-overflow-qualifies-for-the-2035-and-2045-sodrp-targets\"\u003e3.2.2.3 Assessing whether a storm overflow qualifies for the 2035 and 2045 \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e targets\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e has provided the criteria in this section. These identify whether discharges into, or within a certain distance of, any of the ‘high priority sites’ listed would typically qualify for the associated 2035 and 2045 \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e targets.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eImpact modelling cannot be used to prevent a storm overflow site from qualifying as a ‘high priority site’ under the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAny questions regarding specific assets should be directed to the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch6 id=\"criteria-for-high-priority-sites-for-the-ecological-target\"\u003eCriteria for ‘high priority sites’ for the ecological target\u003c/h6\u003e\u003cp\u003eA storm overflow qualifies as a ‘high priority site’ under the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e if it discharges:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003einto or within 50m (inland) or 1km (transitional and coastal waters) of an \u003cabbr title=\"site of special scientific interest\"\u003eSSSI\u003c/abbr\u003e water feature – regardless of whether the water body has favourable or unfavourable status\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003einto or within 50m (inland) or 1km (transitional and coastal waters) of an \u003cabbr title=\"special area of conservation\"\u003eSAC\u003c/abbr\u003e, \u003cabbr title=\"special protection area\"\u003eSPA\u003c/abbr\u003e or Ramsar water feature – regardless of whether the water body has favourable or unfavourable status\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003einto or within 50m (inland) or 1km (transitional and coastal waters) of a chalk stream\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003einto or within 1km from the hydraulic continuity of an \u003cabbr title=\"marine conservation zone\"\u003eMCZ\u003c/abbr\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch6 id=\"waters-currently-failing-ecological-standards-due-to-storm-overflows\"\u003eWaters currently failing ecological standards due to storm overflows\u003c/h6\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e requires water and sewerage companies to demonstrate that their storm overflows are having no adverse ecological impact.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eTo identify sites which are having an adverse impact, water and sewerage companies should refer to the river basin planning ‘reasons for not achieving good status’ (\u003cabbr title=\"reasons for not achieving good status\"\u003eRNAGS\u003c/abbr\u003e) category. This is made up of \u003cabbr title=\"reasons for not achieving good status\"\u003eRNAGS\u003c/abbr\u003e and the most recent \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflow assessment framework\"\u003eSOAF\u003c/abbr\u003e (version 1 or version 2) environmental impact assessments.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eStorm overflows should be prioritised to meet the 2035 and 2045 targets if:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ean assessment finds that storm overflow discharges are a confirmed or probable ‘reason for not achieving good status’\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ean assessment finds that there is an environmental impact through Stage 2 of the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflow assessment framework\"\u003eSOAF\u003c/abbr\u003e version 2\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch6 id=\"shellfish-water-protected-areas\"\u003eShellfish water protected areas\u003c/h6\u003e\u003cp\u003eA storm overflow qualifies as a high priority site under the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e in relation to ‘designated shellfish waters’, if the discharge is into, or within 1km of hydraulic continuity of, a designated shellfish water.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch6 id=\"ecological-standard-for-inland-waters\"\u003eEcological standard for inland waters\u003c/h6\u003e\u003cp\u003eInland waters or freshwaters are defined as those upstream of the tidal limit in estuaries.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e‘No local adverse ecological impact’ means achieving the \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://fwr.org/publication/urban-pollution-manual-upm/\"\u003eUrban Pollution Manual (fwr.org)\u003c/a\u003e fundamental intermittent standards (\u003cabbr title=\"fundamental intermittent standards\"\u003eFIS\u003c/abbr\u003e) and 99 percentile standards downstream of the storm overflow discharge point. The \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e’s \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflow assessment framework\"\u003eSOAF\u003c/abbr\u003e version 2 contains more information on using the \u003cabbr title=\"fundamental intermittent standards\"\u003eFIS\u003c/abbr\u003e and 99 percentile standards to determine impact.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAchievement of urban pollution management (\u003cabbr title=\"urban pollution management\"\u003eUPM\u003c/abbr\u003e) \u003cabbr title=\"fundamental intermittent standards\"\u003eFIS\u003c/abbr\u003e and 99 percentile standards is considered sufficient to prevent harm that would cause a water body to not achieve good ecological status resulting from storm overflow impact. Macroinvertebrate monitoring may be considered in some circumstances to support water quality modelling results. Further detail is set out in \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflow assessment framework\"\u003eSOAF\u003c/abbr\u003e version 2.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf a storm overflow is resulting in these standards being breached, improvements should be secured in line with the timeframes set out in the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch6 id=\"applying-the-upm-framework-to-inland-waters\"\u003eApplying the \u003cabbr title=\"urban pollution management\"\u003eUPM\u003c/abbr\u003e framework to inland waters\u003c/h6\u003e\u003cp\u003eAll work affecting storm overflows should be planned using the \u003cabbr title=\"urban pollution management\"\u003eUPM\u003c/abbr\u003e procedure outlined in \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://fwr.org/publication/urban-pollution-manual-upm/\"\u003esection 3 of the Urban Pollution Manual\u003c/a\u003e. The \u003cabbr title=\"urban pollution management\"\u003eUPM\u003c/abbr\u003e procedure is used to ensure that wastewater discharges from sewer and sewage treatment systems in wet weather meet the ecological requirements of the receiving water in a cost-effective way.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe water sector’s good practice guides such as the \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.ciwem.org/special-interest-groups/urban-drainage-group\"\u003eguidance notes and codes of practice\u003c/a\u003e published by the \u003cabbr title=\"Chartered Institution of Water and Environmental Management\"\u003eCIWEM\u003c/abbr\u003e Urban Drainage Group, should be used to inform the detail of how to build, verify and apply \u003cabbr title=\"urban pollution management\"\u003eUPM\u003c/abbr\u003e modelling techniques.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch6 id=\"ecological-standards-for-coastal-and-estuarine-waters\"\u003eEcological standards for coastal and estuarine waters\u003c/h6\u003e\u003cp\u003eDue to the technical challenges of developing an ecological standard for coastal and estuarine waters, a standard is not currently available.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eUntil a suitable standard is developed and confirmed, water and sewerage companies should plan improvements to storm overflows discharging to coastal and estuarine waters based on the target of not more than an average of 10 spills per annum. This is equivalent to the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e rainfall target and mirrors the long-established surrogate for the environment quality standards to protect shellfisheries.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"public-health-target\"\u003e3.2.3 Public health target\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e set an objective to protect the health of water users through the public health target:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e“Water companies must significantly reduce harmful pathogens from storm overflows discharging near designated bathing waters, by either: applying disinfection; or reducing the frequency of discharges to meet \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e spill standards by 2035.”\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"ea-bathing-water-spill-standards\"\u003e3.2.3.1 \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e bathing water spill standards\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e spill standards are different for inland and coastal bathing waters.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor designated inland (rivers, lakes, and estuaries) bathing waters, storm overflows discharging directly into, or within 5km upstream of the upper limit of, the inland bathing water reach must be designed to achieve no more than an average of one spill per bathing season.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor coastal waters, storm overflows discharging within 1km upstream (and in hydraulic continuity) of designated bathing sites, must be designed to achieve:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eno more than 3 spills per bathing season on average for ‘good’, ‘sufficient’ or ‘poor’ status\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eno more than 2 spills per bathing season on average for ‘excellent’ status\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003e‘Average’ for design purposes should be assessed over a minimum of 10 years.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eDesignated bathing waters in estuaries should be designed to the same standards as those for coastal bathing waters, with the exception that where there is evidence that the designated bathing water is near the upstream freshwater limit and low salinities are observed, then these waters should be given the same protection as rivers (one spill per bathing season).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWater and sewerage companies should design to meet the coastal standards unless advised otherwise by the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFurther investigation by the water company will be required when a specific receiving water is not meeting bathing water standards despite nearby storm overflows meeting individual spill standards. For example, no more than 2 spills per bathing season on average for an ‘excellent’ bathing water.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn addition to the criteria above, the following apply:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eif there is substantive evidence that concludes that bathing water quality is limited by the discharges from storm overflows that are located further away from the designated bathing water site than the distances set out above, the relevant investigation triggers listed above apply\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhen the relevant \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e spill targets for human health are achieved, disinfection of discharges can be used to enhance water quality to meet bathing water standards – this is a clarification of the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e’s targets\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eSection 7 of this document sets out  spill standards in relation to soffit level (the level corresponding to the top of the outfall pipe).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"requirement-for-additional-works\"\u003e3.2.3.2 Requirement for additional works\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eFollowing completion of the spill reduction works, it may be found that the receiving water is not achieving its target public health quality as a result of storm overflow discharges.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn this situation, the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e should consider requiring the water and sewerage company to undertake an investigation and remedial scheme to secure no impacts on human health. In the first instance, this should be based on applying marine impact modelling to meet the following environmental quality standards (\u003cabbr title=\"environmental quality standards\"\u003eEQS\u003c/abbr\u003e).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTable: \u003cabbr title=\"environmental quality standards\"\u003eEQS\u003c/abbr\u003e for faecal bacteria in coastal bathing waters\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ctable\u003e\n  \u003cthead\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"col\"\u003eBathing water class (2006 Bathing Water Directive)\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"col\"\u003eE. Coli standard (colony forming unit (CFU) per 100ml)\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"col\"\u003eIntestinal enterococci standard (CFU per 100ml)\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"col\"\u003eStandard type\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"col\"\u003eMaximum exceedance threshold (% of bathing season duration)\u003c/th\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n  \u003c/thead\u003e\n  \u003ctbody\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eSufficient\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003e500\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003e185\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003e90-percentile\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003e1.8\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eGood\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003e500\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003e200\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003e95-percentile\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003e1.8\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eExcellent\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003e250\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003e100\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003e95-percentile\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003e1.8\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n  \u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\u003cp\u003eThese standards apply to any location within the coastal water, not just the monitoring point. For standards for rivers and lakes, contact the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWater and sewerage companies should not use these approaches to justify increasing spills above the default spills thresholds or existing levels.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"rainfall-target\"\u003e3.2.4 Rainfall target\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e rainfall target will ensure improvement of all storm overflows:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e“Storm overflows will not be permitted to discharge above an average of 10 rainfall events per year by 2050.”\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe maximum average 10 rainfall events target translates to water and sewerage companies designing, operating and maintaining their storm overflows and associated sewerage systems to ensure there are no more than 10 spills per year on average over a 10-year period. This is not limited to spills caused by rainfall.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e rainfall target should not be interpreted as allowing an increase in spills up to 10 spills on average per year, such as due to the deterioration of asset performance.\u003c/p\u003e"
      }
