      "@type": "Question",
      "name": "4. Assessing storm overflows",
      "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/storm-overflows-policy-and-guidance/storm-overflows-policy-and-guidance#assessing-storm-overflows",
      "acceptedAnswer": {
        "@type": "Answer",
        "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/storm-overflows-policy-and-guidance/storm-overflows-policy-and-guidance#assessing-storm-overflows",
        "text": "\u003cp\u003eAs set out in Section 2, water and sewerage companies must return event duration monitoring data annually to the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e for every storm overflow operated by a sewerage undertaker whose area is wholly or mainly in England. The data must contain the frequency and duration of all storm overflow spills.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis is a key step in water and sewerage companies and regulators being able to identify:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhich storm overflows should be investigated\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhere subsequent improvements are required\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis section provides an overarching approach to storm overflow investigations as agreed with the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e and Ofwat. Where needed, this may be complemented by further guidance from the regulators outlining technical detail on investigations.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt is ultimately the responsibility of water and sewerage companies to understand the obligations they need to meet and deliver action to achieve these. There may be circumstances in which ensuring compliance requires water and sewerage companies to go further than guidance set out by government or regulators.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"investigation-triggers\"\u003e4.1 Investigation triggers\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eA number of requirements need to be considered by water and sewerage companies when evaluating their assets. Assets can include storm overflows on the network or at wastewater treatment works.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eInvestigations are a common mechanism through which water and sewerage companies and regulators can:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eevaluate an asset\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003econsider which requirements might apply\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edetermine whether action is required to deliver improvements\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThere are currently around 14,500 storm overflows in England. Given the number of assets, it is reasonable for regulators to establish triggers for investigations in order to:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eensure that resources are used efficiently\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eassist water and sewerage companies with prioritising the work which needs to be completed to achieve compliance with requirements in the most effective manner\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflow assessment framework\"\u003eSOAF\u003c/abbr\u003e version 2, the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e sets triggers based on the frequency of spills to prioritise investigations in respect of the highest spilling storm overflows.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThrough its enforcement proceedings, Ofwat has suggested a series of performance indicators, including spill levels. These should act as triggers for water and sewerage companies to proactively consider whether there may be compliance issues now or in the foreseeable future. Such consideration is part of water and sewerage companies’ obligations to ensure their assets are performing sufficiently.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e and Ofwat investigation triggers align to form a complementary regulatory framework. If a storm overflow met or exceeded an investigation trigger set by the regulators, the water and sewerage company would be responsible for navigating the investigation process in section 4.2 and the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e’s \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflow assessment framework\"\u003eSOAF\u003c/abbr\u003e version 2.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt is important to note that there is no single spill trigger set in law at which an investigation is required. While investigations can be triggered by meeting or exceeding a threshold, this is not the only route for identifying the need for improvements to be made to a storm overflow.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWater and sewerage companies have a responsibility to investigate a storm overflow discharging outside of ‘exceptional circumstances’, regardless of whether the asset has exceeded a spill trigger, as set out in Section 3.1.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRegulators may also decide to investigate water and sewerage companies and take enforcement action in circumstances other than those described in this document. For example, a storm overflow may not meet an investigation trigger, but if a permit condition were breached then the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e could investigate and take enforcement action in line with the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e’s enforcement and sanctions policy.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn addition to these investigation triggers, water and sewerage company \u003cabbr title=\"drainage and wastewater management plans\"\u003eDWMPs\u003c/abbr\u003e contain spill ‘risk thresholds’ for strategic planning purposes. \u003cabbr title=\"drainage and wastewater management plan\"\u003eDWMP\u003c/abbr\u003e risk thresholds use observed and modelled spills to forecast storm overflow performance, and investment needed, into the future.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe investigation triggers described in this document, Ofwat’s enforcement cases and the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e’s \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflow assessment framework\"\u003eSOAF\u003c/abbr\u003e version 2 alert water and sewerage companies to more immediate issues with individual assets. These should be addressed to bring assets into compliance or prevent at risk assets becoming unsatisfactory or non-compliant, while \u003cabbr title=\"drainage and wastewater management plan\"\u003eDWMP\u003c/abbr\u003e risk thresholds allow them to strategically plan investment and build resilience into their networks.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"investigation-process\"\u003e4.2 Investigation process\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe investigation process involves gathering information and using this to understand the factors that have contributed to a storm overflow discharging and the impacts that the discharges are having.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eTo determine whether improvements may be required, water and sewerage companies should consider on a case-by-case basis:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eall relevant legal requirements\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003etargets in the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eany other non-legislative requirements for their assets\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eWater and sewerage companies should also consider whether there are deadlines by which these requirements must be met.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThrough Ofwat’s price review business plan cycle, water and sewerage companies allocate funds for investigations against their statutory and non-statutory requirements. They will then schedule these during the asset management plan (\u003cabbr title=\"asset management plan\"\u003eAMP\u003c/abbr\u003e) period in the most efficient way.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhere requirements for investigations emerge outside of the price review business planning process, such as mid-\u003cabbr title=\"asset management plan\"\u003eAMP\u003c/abbr\u003e, water and sewerage companies should aim to carry these out as soon as feasibly possible. Where relevant, priority must be given to scheduling investigations which are linked to statutory requirements. For \u003cabbr title=\"2024 price review\"\u003ePR24\u003c/abbr\u003e, further information is provided in Ofwat’s final determination documentation, which explains the storm overflows uncertainty mechanism they have put in place.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eInvestigations should be reviewed by companies periodically. Section 3.1.5 provides more information on the factors that may highlight the need to review a \u003cabbr title=\"best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs\"\u003eBTKNEEC\u003c/abbr\u003e test or an investigation.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflow assessment framework\"\u003eSOAF\u003c/abbr\u003e version 2 outlines in detail the investigation process to be followed for storm overflows under the \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994 for both \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e and Ofwat investigation triggers.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"identifying-improvements\"\u003e4.3 Identifying improvements\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eAs part of the investigation process, water and sewerage companies should develop and assess their options for improving a storm overflow, taking a number of different factors into consideration, as set out in this section and in the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e’s \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflow assessment framework\"\u003eSOAF\u003c/abbr\u003e version 2.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf an appropriate improvement is identified, the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e will include improvement conditions in the permit to meet appropriate standards as soon as practicable. In some circumstances, the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e may identify a storm overflow as impacting the environment or human health outside of the usual investigation process proactively require improvements through permit variation.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe process of identifying potential improvements is not limited to the 5-yearly price review cycle. At times, water and sewerage companies will be required to develop and assess their options for improving storm overflows more frequently, to comply with their legal obligations.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"optioneering\"\u003e4.3.1 Optioneering\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eWater and sewerage companies should be able to demonstrate to regulators that they have considered a range of options when identifying and designing their schemes to improve storm overflows. This could include:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003egrey infrastructure\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003egreen infrastructure\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003egrey and green hybrid improvements\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eimprovements to reduce demands on sewerage assets\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eimprovements that increase capacity\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003einnovative alternative improvements\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eWater and sewerage companies should consider not only the capital and operational (Totex) costs of improvements, but also the carbon (embedded and operational) and additional societal and nature-based benefits of each option.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt is important that standards, assessments and upgrades focus on the site or specific overflow under consideration. However, when deciding on options, water and sewerage companies should consider a catchment approach alongside an asset-by-asset approach where appropriate. This is not a new expectation: companies should already be applying a catchment approach in other areas of planning, such as in \u003cabbr title=\"drainage and wastewater management plans\"\u003eDWMPs\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor example, by considering the benefits that storm overflow improvements may offer on a wider level than just the individual asset, particularly where there are significant environmental issues which cannot be improved in a cost beneficial way simply by remediating one asset.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhen deciding on and comparing options, water and sewerage companies should also consider the different timeframes for delivery, particularly if there is a regulatory deadline.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"optioneering-based-on-wastewater-supply-and-demand-modelling\"\u003e4.3.2 Optioneering based on wastewater supply and demand modelling\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eWater and sewerage company optioneering of storm overflow improvements should consider demand- as well as supply-based options within the context of wastewater supply demand (also known as wastewater flow or capacity). \u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSupply-based options, such as increasing capacity of the sewerage network or increased treatment capacity, usually rely upon grey infrastructure, or in some cases a hybrid grey and green infrastructure, such as constructed wetlands. \u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eDemand-based options, including surface water diversion away from combined sewers or its attenuation, are considered more sustainable as they relieve pressure on sewerage systems now and in the future, whereas supply-based options often require upgrading as pressures increase in the future. Demand-based options also reduce the ongoing costs of treatment and conveyance (such as pumping), so have smaller revenue costs and smaller operational carbon over their lifetime.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"green-infrastructure\"\u003e4.3.3 Green infrastructure\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e promotes and encourages low carbon and green improvements to addressing storm overflow spills.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eGreen infrastructure and other nature-based improvements can be an effective option to reduce the harm caused by storm overflows and can provide multiple co-benefits for the environment and society. For example, separating surface water so that it does not mix with sewage and is diverted to water gardens or wetlands:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eimproves water quality\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ecreates new habitats for species\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eacts as a carbon sink\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e expects the adoption of green infrastructure, either wholly or partly, to be encouraged by the regulators in line with their own legal duties and where it can meet water and sewerage companies’ legal requirements.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe regulators retain some flexibility when working with water and sewerage companies on the timeframes for delivering green infrastructure improvements (see section 5.2). Water and sewerage companies can further discuss the delivery of green infrastructure improvements with the regulators as needed, on a site or catchment basis.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWater and sewerage companies should investigate and introduce green infrastructure at the upstream end of catchments. This is linked to the expectation that water and sewerage companies will consider a catchment approach when optioneering, where appropriate (see section 4.3.1). Upstream improvements often provide greater societal benefits and have lower carbon cost compared to green infrastructure implemented in the downstream area of a catchment.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe environmental benefits of green infrastructure projects may take some time to be realised, and so may not be achieved before the target dates specified in the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e. As such, these projects can still be counted towards achieving the targets if they are started before 2027 and delivered as quickly as possible. Promoting the use of green infrastructure to achieve the targets in the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e will continue to be subject to review.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eGreen infrastructure improvements to storm overflows can be both supply- and demand-based. These improvements have advantages in that they can in some cases lead to lower embedded carbon and have lower operational carbon emissions than typical grey infrastructure improvements.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOn the commencement of section 5 of the Water (Special Measures) Act 2025, water and sewerage companies’ statutory \u003cabbr title=\"drainage and wastewater management plans\"\u003eDWMPs\u003c/abbr\u003e will have to detail the use that is to be made of nature-based solutions, technologies and facilities within the undertaker’s drainage system and sewerage system.\u003c/p\u003e"
      }

      "@type": "Question",
      "name": "5. Delivering storm overflow improvements",
      "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/storm-overflows-policy-and-guidance/storm-overflows-policy-and-guidance#delivering-storm-overflow-improvements",
      "acceptedAnswer": {
        "@type": "Answer",
        "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/storm-overflows-policy-and-guidance/storm-overflows-policy-and-guidance#delivering-storm-overflow-improvements",
        "text": "\u003cp\u003eOnce a storm overflow has been assessed under \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflow assessment framework\"\u003eSOAF\u003c/abbr\u003e version 2, and if it has been determined that there is an appropriate solution for improvement, water and sewerage companies must plan and deliver these improvements so that they comply with relevant legal and policy requirements.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e and the regulators understand the need to take into account the deliverability, affordability and financeability of investment required to improve storm overflow performance over time. While meeting regulatory requirements, including fixed regulatory deadlines, must be a water company’s priority, consideration should be given by regulators where appropriate to the timing of improvements being phased over multiple asset management periods.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis will support delivery, ensure affordability to customers, and ensure water and sewerage companies can attract the necessary investment in alignment with \u003cabbr title=\"asset management plan\"\u003eAMP\u003c/abbr\u003e cycles. For the \u003cabbr title=\"2024 price review\"\u003ePR24\u003c/abbr\u003e period, further detail is provided in Ofwat’s final determination documents.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis section suggests considerations for regulators and water and sewerage companies to help ensure improvement plans are affordable, financeable and deliverable.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"improving-storm-overflows-under-the-uwwtr-1994-and-the-sodrp\"\u003e5.1 Improving storm overflows under the \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994 and the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e\n\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994 and the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e share the same overall ambition: to reduce the harm caused by storm overflow discharges. Despite a shared ambition, the action that water and sewerage companies would need to take to meet \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994 requirements may sometimes differ from what is needed to meet \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e targets.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn order to identify which of the drivers requires the most environmentally beneficial results, a storm overflow improvement required under \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994 (having satisfied the \u003cabbr title=\"best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs\"\u003eBTKNEEC\u003c/abbr\u003e test) should be considered alongside other improvements to meet legal requirements and action to meet the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e targets.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor example, an assessment under the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e’s \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflow assessment framework\"\u003eSOAF\u003c/abbr\u003e version 2 could find that in order to satisfy \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994 requirements, a particular storm overflow should be improved so that it spills no more than 13 times per year.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf that same storm overflow was discharging into or near a site of special scientific interest (\u003cabbr title=\"site of special scientific interest\"\u003eSSSI\u003c/abbr\u003e), this would be classed as a ‘high priority site’ under the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e. Under the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e the storm overflow would need to be improved to meet both the ecological target, and the rainfall target.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis might result in the storm overflow needing to be improved so that it spills fewer than 10 times on average per year, or a lower spill frequency to eliminate ecological harm. Its ‘high priority site’ status would also influence the timing of the improvement.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn this case, the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e requirements would be more stringent than the \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e requirements. Taking action in line with the most stringent requirements would result in greater benefits for the environment and public health.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhere possible, \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e recommends that water and sewerage companies design improvement options which fulfil all the relevant requirements for the storm overflow being assessed, minimising situations where multiple improvements are made to the same asset.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThere may be circumstances in which this approach is not feasible or would result in unacceptable delays to compliance with the legislation, and so a more modular approach may therefore be more appropriate.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn all circumstances, water and sewerage companies must fulfil their legal obligations on storm overflows, and as such prioritise the delivery of storm overflow improvements which are required in law.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eUltimately, it is for water and sewerage companies to determine the most effective way of complying with their legal requirements and meeting the targets set out in the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e. The interplay between \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e and \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994 requirements should not be used as a reason to delay improvements.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"timeframes-for-delivery\"\u003e5.2 Timeframes for delivery\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eGovernment expects water and sewerage companies to achieve compliance by delivering improvements as fast as possible, with regulators incentivising and monitoring this delivery.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eGiven the challenges associated with the scale and complexity of investment on storm overflows, with some improvements needing to be delivered over several price review periods, it is important that the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e and Ofwat retain some flexibility when working with water and sewerage companies on the timeframe for improvements.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhen regulators engage with water and sewerage companies on the planning and sequencing of storm overflow improvements, they should give consideration to the following factors:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eprioritisation of storm overflow improvements (for example, meeting legal requirements or target achievement dates)\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eenvironmental and public health outcomes\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edeliverability, affordability and financeability of improvements at a project and programme level\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhen fulfilling their statutory duties on storm overflows, regulators will take all appropriate factors into consideration.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"distinguishing-between-maintenance-improvements-and-longer-term-improvements\"\u003e5.3 Distinguishing between maintenance improvements and longer-term improvements\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn many cases, compliance issues can be addressed through basic operational changes, repairs and maintenance. These types of improvements have been provided for and continue to be provided for through water and sewerage companies’ base revenue allowances and should be reflected in statutory \u003cabbr title=\"drainage and wastewater management plans\"\u003eDWMPs\u003c/abbr\u003e on an ongoing basis.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWater and sewerage companies should not delay the implementation of such improvements in favour of a longer-term build solution, or by waiting for annual \u003cabbr title=\"event duration monitor\"\u003eEDM\u003c/abbr\u003e returns where a problem has been identified.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"the-role-of-government-and-regulators-in-overseeing-planning-and-delivery-of-improvements\"\u003e5.4 The role of government and regulators in overseeing planning and delivery of improvements\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eGovernment and regulators have responsibilities in relation to the planning and delivery of improvements and work together to support each other in delivery of their respective remits, consistent with their statutory duties. However, they have different areas of primary focus, reflective of their areas of expertise.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"the-environment-agencys-role-in-planning-and-overseeing-delivery-of-improvements\"\u003e5.4.1 The Environment Agency’s role in planning and overseeing delivery of improvements \u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e takes the lead in identifying the obligations for water and sewerage companies in the water industry strategic environmental requirements (\u003cabbr title=\"water industry strategic environmental requirements\"\u003eWISER\u003c/abbr\u003e) guidance.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"water industry strategic environmental requirements\"\u003eWISER\u003c/abbr\u003e guidance covers the issues and opportunities water and sewerage companies should consider when meeting their environmental obligations, including, but not limited to, improvements on storm overflows.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eObligations identified in the \u003cabbr title=\"water industry strategic environmental requirements\"\u003eWISER\u003c/abbr\u003e guidance for storm overflows then translate into measures and actions identified through the water industry national environment programme (\u003cabbr title=\"water industry national environment programme\"\u003eWINEP\u003c/abbr\u003e).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e works with water and sewerage companies to identify suitable schemes to meet these obligations and reviews draft \u003cabbr title=\"water industry national environment programme\"\u003eWINEP\u003c/abbr\u003e measures ahead of final determination of price review allowances by Ofwat.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e also:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eassesses the progress of these storm overflow improvements by tracking delivery of the \u003cabbr title=\"water industry national environment programme\"\u003eWINEP\u003c/abbr\u003e measures, and where changes are made, effecting these changes in the applicable permits\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eoversees the delivery of the most cost-beneficial solution as identified through the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflow assessment framework\"\u003eSOAF\u003c/abbr\u003e in order to reduce environmental impact, frequency of discharges or both, subject to appropriate prioritisation\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"ofwats-role-in-planning-and-overseeing-delivery-of-improvements\"\u003e5.4.2 Ofwat’s role in planning and overseeing delivery of improvements\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eOfwat takes the lead in setting revenue allowances through their price review for the efficient investment companies need to fulfil their legal obligations and service commitments to customers, including in relation to storm overflows.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis price review process is informed by business plans put forward by water and sewerage companies. These plans are then reviewed by Ofwat as part of their final determination process.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOfwat continues to take into account the affordability, financeability and deliverability of these plans, working with the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e and government as necessary to ensure water and sewerage companies have clarity on their long-term investment requirements and funding landscape.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOfwat also incentivises water and sewerage companies to deliver against their commitments, through:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eperformance commitments\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eprice control deliverables\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ereturning money to customers if these are not delivered\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.ofwat.gov.uk/regulated-companies/price-review/2024-price-review/framework-and-methodology/final-methodology/pr24-performance-commitment-definitions/\"\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"2024 price review\"\u003ePR24\u003c/abbr\u003e includes performance commitments (ofwat.gov.uk)\u003c/a\u003e, with financial consequences based on the average number of storm overflow spills, to encourage water and sewerage companies to address high spilling sites. Through this process, Ofwat will identify:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eworks which are funded through base spend, such as operational and maintenance\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003espill reduction improvements which are funded through enhancement expenditure\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.ofwat.gov.uk/publication/storm-overflows-pc-definition/\"\u003estorm overflows performance commitments definition (ofwat.gov.uk)\u003c/a\u003e  was published in June 2023.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"defras-role-in-planning-and-overseeing-and-delivery-of-improvements\"\u003e5.4.3 \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e’s role in planning and overseeing and delivery of improvements\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eAmong other things, \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e has responsibility for setting the overall direction of storm overflows policy, including targets and legislation.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis includes issuing strategic policy statements to Ofwat, outlining \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e’s priorities for the regulation of the water industry ahead of price reviews.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThrough this process, \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e seeks to ensure clarity and predictability for the sector, consulting on any significant changes at the earliest stage, to ensure water and sewerage companies have the stability they need for their long-term planning and to secure a pipeline of investment for the required improvements.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e also signs off the water industry strategic environmental requirements (\u003cabbr title=\"water industry strategic environmental requirements\"\u003eWISER\u003c/abbr\u003e).\u003c/p\u003e"

        "text": "\u003cp\u003eWhere there are legal requirements in relation to storm overflows or the discharges from them, it is the responsibility of water and sewerage companies to:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eunderstand those requirements\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eassess whether the design and operation of their assets comply with the requirements\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003etake necessary action in an appropriate timeframe to ensure that they are, and remain, in compliance with those requirements\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf there are concerns about non-compliance, it is for the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e and Ofwat to take appropriate steps to investigate further and take enforcement action where appropriate.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"the-environment-agencys-role-in-storm-overflow-enforcement\"\u003e6.1 The Environment Agency’s role in storm overflow enforcement \u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e’s role in relation to enforcement includes:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eexercising their duty under regulation 6 of the \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994 to carry out their functions under the \u003cabbr title=\"Environmental Permitting (England and Wales) Regulations 2016\"\u003eEPR 2016\u003c/abbr\u003e to secure limitation of pollution of receiving waters due to storm water overflows – this duty is applicable when the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e is exercising their enforcement functions\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003etaking enforcement action where they are satisfied that a permit condition has been breached, in accordance with their enforcement and sanctions policy – enforcement action may result in enforcement notices, civil sanctions or criminal prosecutions\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"ofwats-role-in-storm-overflow-enforcement\"\u003e6.2 Ofwat’s role in storm overflow enforcement\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eOfwat’s role in relation to enforcement includes fulfilling their duty under section 18 of the \u003cabbr title=\"Water Industry Act 1991\"\u003eWIA 1991\u003c/abbr\u003e to impose an enforcement order on a company where they are satisfied that there is, or is likely to be, a breach of either:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003esection 94 of the \u003cabbr title=\"Water Industry Act 1991\"\u003eWIA 1991\u003c/abbr\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eregulation 4 of the \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eSuch an enforcement order is to secure the company’s compliance.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSection 19 of the \u003cabbr title=\"Water Industry Act 1991\"\u003eWIA 1991\u003c/abbr\u003e provides exceptions to Ofwat’s duty under section 18, where the breach is of a trivial nature. It also provides an exception where either:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe company has given and is complying with an undertaking to secure its compliance\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ean enforcement order would be inconsistent with Ofwat’s duties under Chapter 2 of Part 1 \u003cabbr title=\"Water Industry Act 1991\"\u003eWIA 1991\u003c/abbr\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf a company fails to comply with such an undertaking, Ofwat has a duty under section 18 of the \u003cabbr title=\"Water Industry Act 1991\"\u003eWIA 1991\u003c/abbr\u003e to impose an enforcement order to secure compliance.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSection 22A of the \u003cabbr title=\"Water Industry Act 1991\"\u003eWIA 1991\u003c/abbr\u003e allows Ofwat to impose financial penalties, where they are satisfied that a company has breached or is breaching a relevant legal obligation. Ofwat will consider a number of factors in determining the appropriate level of such a penalty in the circumstances of each breach. Financial penalties imposed in accordance with this provision cannot exceed 10% of a company’s relevant turnover in the preceding business year.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOn a case-by-case basis, and where their powers allow them to do so, Ofwat will consider regulatory settlement. Where accepted, this would require an undertaking to be agreed, setting out:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe remedial steps Ofwat considers appropriate to secure compliance\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eappropriate financial and non-financial commitments, such as a redress package for customers or remediation of harm caused by the identified breach\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eSuch regulatory settlement may be accepted in lieu of all or part of a proposed financial penalty.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eBefore making an enforcement order or imposing a financial penalty, Ofwat is required to consider whether it would be more appropriate to proceed using their powers under the Competition Act 1998.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"defras-role-in-storm-overflow-enforcement\"\u003e6.3 \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e’s role in storm overflow enforcement\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e’s role includes:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eresponsibility for setting the overall direction of storm overflows policy, including targets and legislation\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003egeneral strategic oversight of the storm overflows regulatory system\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eestablishing the strategic policy direction and the overarching legislative framework within which regulators operate and ensuring these remain up to date with the best available information on environmental needs and the water industry\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis includes issuing strategic policy statements to Ofwat outlining \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e’s priorities for the regulation of the water industry ahead of price reviews. Ofwat has a legal duty to carry out their functions in accordance with a strategic policy statement, as set out in section 2A of the \u003cabbr title=\"Water Industry Act 1991\"\u003eWIA 1991\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e also meets regularly with the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e and Ofwat to retain an understanding of:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewater and sewerage company performance\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow the regulators are exercising their enforcement duties more generally\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis is while ensuring that the regulators retain required independence on individual cases and enforcement proceedings.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e recognises the jurisdiction of the regulators in enforcing compliance with relevant statutory or non-statutory requirements.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAs an example, \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e expects the regulators to utilise data on storm overflows obtained via \u003cabbr title=\"event duration monitors\"\u003eEDMs\u003c/abbr\u003e (and other relevant monitoring programmes as they become available) to inform their assessment of water company performance and compliance. However, it is for the regulators to decide:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhich other sources of information are necessary in order to form a view on these matters\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow any investigation processes should be carried out\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eultimately what the outcome of these investigations are\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e"

        "text": "\u003cp\u003eDraft guidance on the \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994 was issued to dischargers and regulators in July 1997 (the 1997 guidance). It was intended as a working document on the implementation and interpretation of the \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eExcept for a limited update in 2009, the 1997 guidance has not been revised since it was published. As discussed throughout this document, there have been considerable changes in the storm overflows policy landscape in recent years, including the issuance of the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e and increased awareness and evidence due to 100% storm overflow \u003cabbr title=\"event duration monitor\"\u003eEDM\u003c/abbr\u003e coverage. In addition, technical knowledge relating to water quality has progressed.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWithin the 1997 guidance, information related to storm overflows is largely contained within Annex 8, entitled ‘Framework for Consenting Intermittent Discharges’. Annex 3, entitled ‘Design, Construction and Operation of Collecting Systems and Treatment Plant’, also refers to the operation of storm overflows (as part of the wider sewerage system).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAll of Annex 8 to the 1997 guidance, to the extent that it had not already been superseded, is now withdrawn in respect of storm overflows operated by water and sewerage companies whose areas are wholly or mainly in England, and superseded by this publication in 2025. This does not apply to storm overflows operated by water and sewerage companies whose areas are wholly or mainly in Wales.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWe have also provided updated references for the design, construction and operation of collecting systems, in place of the references found in Annex 3 of the 1997 guidance.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe rest of the 1997 guidance is not being withdrawn at this stage but may be updated in future.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe following sections have been provided by the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e, as the technical expert on storm overflows regulation. Further updates to the sections below may be provided by the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e as appropriate.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"helpful-references-for-the-design-construction-and-operation-of-collecting-systems\"\u003e7.1 Helpful references for the design, construction and operation of collecting systems\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe principal document that defines current practice for the design, construction and operation of collecting systems is BS EN 752:2017 “Drain and sewer systems outside buildings – sewer system management”. Other relevant supporting documentation includes:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://fwr.org/publication/urban-pollution-manual-upm/\"\u003eUrban Pollution Management 3rd Edition (2018)\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.ciwem.org/assets/uploads/CIWEM_UDG_EDM_Good_Practice_Guide_2021_final.pdf\"\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Chartered Institution of Water and Environmental Management\"\u003eCIWEM\u003c/abbr\u003e Event Duration Monitoring Good Practice Guide\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/review-of-urban-pollution-management-standards-against-water-framework-directive-requirements\"\u003ereview of urban pollution management standards against \u003cabbr title=\"Water Framework Directive\"\u003eWFD\u003c/abbr\u003e requirements\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.ciwem.org/special-interest-groups/urban-drainage-group\"\u003eguidance notes and codes of practice published by the \u003cabbr title=\"Chartered Institution of Water and Environmental Management\"\u003eCIWEM\u003c/abbr\u003e Urban Drainage Group\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edrainage and wastewater management plan guidelines\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eA number of documents deal with storm overflows and use of rainfall time series for sewer system modelling. These include the following:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.ciwem.org/assets/pdf/Special%20Interest%20Groups/Urban%20Drainage%20Group/CIWEM-UDG-Rainfall-Guide-2016.pdf\"\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Chartered Institution of Water and Environmental Management\"\u003eCIWEM\u003c/abbr\u003e Rainfall Modelling Guide\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.ciwem.org/assets/pdf/Special%20Interest%20Groups/Urban%20Drainage%20Group/Code%20of%20Practice%20for%20the%20Hydraulic%20Modelling%20of%20Ur.pdf\"\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Chartered Institution of Water and Environmental Management\"\u003eCIWEM\u003c/abbr\u003e Code of Practice for the Hydraulic Modelling of Urban Drainage Systems\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://ukwir.org/eng/reports/15-CL-10-16-1/129641/Rainfall-Intensity-for-Sewer-Design--Technical-Guide\"\u003eUK Water Industry Research (\u003cabbr title=\"UK Water Industry Research\"\u003eUKWIR\u003c/abbr\u003e) Rainfall Intensity for Sewer Design - Technical Guide\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://ukwir.org/eng/climate-change-rainfall-for-use-in-sewerage-design-design-storm-profiles-antecedent-conditions-redup-tool-update-and-seasonality-impacts-guidance\"\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"UK Water Industry Research\"\u003eUKWIR\u003c/abbr\u003e Climate Change Rainfall for use in Sewerage Design – Design Storm Profiles, Antecedent Conditions, RED-UP Tool Update and Seasonality Impacts Guidance\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e uses the \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://ukwir.org/ukwir-redup-tool\"\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"UK Water Industry Research\"\u003eUKWIR\u003c/abbr\u003e RED-UP\u003c/a\u003e tool for creating climate perturbed rainfall time series in the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflow assessment framework\"\u003eSOAF\u003c/abbr\u003e version 2, and \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.ceh.ac.uk/our-science/projects/eflag-enhanced-future-flows-and-groundwater\"\u003eeFLaG\u003c/a\u003e for guidance on flow. Separate guidance will be available for surface water temperature uplifts once published.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eReference should be made to the \u003cabbr title=\"Chartered Institution of Water and Environmental Management\"\u003eCIWEM\u003c/abbr\u003e Urban Drainage Group guidance ‘\u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.ciwem.org/assets/pdf/Special%20Interest%20Groups/Urban%20Drainage%20Group/The-Design-of-CSO-Chambers-to-Incorporate-Screens.pdf\"\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Wastewater Planning Users Group\"\u003eWaPUG\u003c/abbr\u003e Guide: The Design of \u003cabbr title=\"combined sewer overflow\"\u003eCSO\u003c/abbr\u003e Chambers to Incorporate Screens’\u003c/a\u003e and any future updates of this.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"framework-for-permitting-storm-overflows\"\u003e7.2 Framework for permitting storm overflows\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"introduction-1\"\u003e7.2.1 Introduction\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis section sets out criteria for the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e’s permitting of those overflows that are unsatisfactory. This is not a complete methodology for determining permit or \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e compliance. It is intended as a guideline to provide clarity for water and sewerage companies. Companies should also refer to the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e’s latest guidance and relevant legal requirements.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eUnsettled storm overflows at sewage treatment works will be considered in the same manner as network storm overflows under the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e. Clearly, if one is unsatisfactory according to the criteria below, it should be treated in the same way as any other storm overflow, but this may need to be tied in with a review of the permit for the whole works.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"definition-of-unsatisfactory-and-at-risk-storm-overflows\"\u003e7.2.2 Definition of ‘unsatisfactory’ and ‘at risk’ storm overflows\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe following table is to be used by the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e in deciding which storm overflows are unsatisfactory and, therefore, subject to permit review to drive improvements.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe criteria given in the table below are largely objective, although some subjectivity may apply. In particular, some discretion must be left for local interpretation of the significance and contribution of an overflow to a particular problem.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eCriteria to identify ‘at risk storm overflows’ are set out in the table in this section. These overflows are not yet unsatisfactory but are at risk of becoming unsatisfactory if action is not taken as they currently cross accepted performance thresholds, however the timeframe to improve them to meet these thresholds set out in plans has not yet been exceeded.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eExamples of situations where a storm overflow could be considered ‘at risk’ of becoming unsatisfactory include where:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eit does not meet set standards of engineering and aesthetic control for storm overflows (for example, no screen yet installed) but not yet passed the date specified in the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e for all storm overflows to be screened\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ecurrent spill performance exceeds thresholds set in the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflow assessment framework\"\u003eSOAF\u003c/abbr\u003e, but the investigation (which is being progressed) has not yet concluded that spill reduction is required\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ecurrent spill performance exceeds thresholds set in the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e, but not yet passed the date specified in the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e for all storm overflows to meet these thresholds\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethere is confirmed local adverse ecological impact, but not yet passed the relevant date in the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e for the storm overflow to meet these thresholds\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eit does not have sufficient hydraulic capacity compared to accepted minimum design standards\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eIssues identified through an investigation into an at risk overflow that could result in the storm overflow becoming unsatisfactory should be addressed proactively. Issues identified that are not sufficient to risk the storm overflow becoming unsatisfactory should be reflected in and addressed as part of subsequent integrated programmes of work within the catchments, including \u003cabbr title=\"drainage and wastewater management plans\"\u003eDWMPs\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf an overflow becomes unsatisfactory, the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e can review the water and sewerage company’s permit or take enforcement action if there is a breach of the existing permit.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e can include an improvement condition in permits for unsatisfactory storm overflows to meet the appropriate standards as soon as practicable.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"water industry national environment programme\"\u003eWINEP\u003c/abbr\u003e investigations and improvements should be aligned to achieve the targets set out in the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e through the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e’s \u003cabbr title=\"water industry national environment programme\"\u003eWINEP\u003c/abbr\u003e guidance prior to each \u003cabbr title=\"asset management plan\"\u003eAMP\u003c/abbr\u003e cycle.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ctable\u003e\n  \u003cthead\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"col\"\u003eRequirement\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003cth pollution of groundwater\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eNot applicable\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eNot applicable\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eNot applicable\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"row\"\u003eAsset standard\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eNone\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eNot applicable\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eDoes not have sufficient hydraulic capacity compared to accepted minimum design standards\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eFormula A \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e3PG+ I + 3E \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eGroundwater inundated sewerage system\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n  \u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"definitions-to-inform-the-permitting-of-storm-overflows\"\u003e7.2.3 Definitions to inform the permitting of storm overflows\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe following definitions are relevant for storm overflows discharging into freshwater, coastal waters and estuaries.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"dry-weather-flow-dwf\"\u003eDry weather flow (\u003cabbr title=\"dry weather flow\"\u003eDWF\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor design purposes \u003cabbr title=\"dry weather flow\"\u003eDWF\u003c/abbr\u003e is calculated by the equation ‘\u003cabbr title=\"dry weather flow\"\u003eDWF\u003c/abbr\u003e = PG + I\u003csub\u003eMAX\u003c/sub\u003e + E’, where:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eP = population served\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eG = water consumption per head per day\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eI\u003csub\u003eMAX\u003c/sub\u003e = maximum infiltration rate over the whole year\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eE = trade effluent flow to sewer as applicable\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"formula-a\"\u003eFormula A\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eFormula A is a storm overflow setting as defined in the Report of the Technical Committee on Storm Overflows and the Disposal of Storm Sewage (1970).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe formula should be amended, as described in the report, for any separate areas within the sewer catchment. Where storage is provided at a storm overflow, and in very large sewerage systems where significant smoothing of flows occurs, this will be taken into account in defining the performance equivalent to ‘Formula A’ without storage.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe standard ‘Formula A’ is \u003cabbr title=\"dry weather flow\"\u003eDWF\u003c/abbr\u003e + 1360P + 2E, where flows are expressed in litres per day, but minor local variations have been developed and are acceptable provided they are fully documented.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"soffit-level\"\u003eSoffit level\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eSoffit level is the level of the top inner surface of the outfall pipe.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"mean-low-water-of-spring-tides-mlws\"\u003eMean low water of spring tides (\u003cabbr title=\"mean low water level of springtides\"\u003eMLWS\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"mean low water level of springtides\"\u003eMLWS\u003c/abbr\u003e is the level of ‘mean low water spring tides’ as given in the Admiralty Tide Tables and corrected, where necessary, for the actual location of the outfall.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"estuarine-waters\"\u003eEstuarine waters\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eEstuarine waters are all waters defined as estuarine in regulation 2(1) of the \u003cabbr title=\"Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations\"\u003eUWWTR\u003c/abbr\u003e 1994.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"coastal-waters\"\u003eCoastal waters\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eCoastal waters are all marine waters up to the 3 nautical mile limit, excluding estuaries.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"normal-requirements-for-storm-overflows\"\u003e7.2.4 Normal requirements for storm overflows\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe following requirements will normally apply to water and sewerage companies with storm overflows which discharge into freshwaters. The \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e will assess whether companies are complying with these requirements. This list is non-exhaustive.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe sewerage system must be designed so that discharges are not made until the incoming flow exceeds that calculated from ‘Formula A’, as defined above.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe discharge should not create any visual or aesthetic impact caused by solids, paper, plastic or fungus as demonstrated by a history of justified public complaints or concern.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAs set out in the \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e, water and sewerage companies should install 6mm screens on every storm overflow when making improvements to meet \u003cabbr title=\"storm overflows discharge reduction plan\"\u003eSODRP\u003c/abbr\u003e targets.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eScreening controls are defined as 6mm solids separation: separation from the effluent, of a significant quantity of persistent material, and faecal and organic solids, greater than 6mm in any 2 dimensions. Screens should be designed to operate effectively up to the 1 in 5-year flow rate.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eScreens should be installed into a chamber which meets the latest design guidance available.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe normal minimum design requirement is for all sewage flows up to 3PG + I\u003csub\u003eMAX\u003c/sub\u003e + 3E to be fully treated (flow to full treatment (\u003cabbr title=\"flow to full treatment\"\u003eFFT\u003c/abbr\u003e)). Flow between \u003cabbr title=\"flow to full treatment\"\u003eFFT\u003c/abbr\u003e (normally designed at 3PG + I\u003csub\u003eMAX\u003c/sub\u003e + 3E) and 6PG + I\u003csub\u003eMAX\u003c/sub\u003e + 3E or Formula A should normally have tank treatment provided by storm tank capacity of 68 l per hd or 2 hours at 3PG + I\u003csub\u003eMAX\u003c/sub\u003e + 3E as appropriate or by a process giving equivalent performance. Flows greater than 6PG + I\u003csub\u003eMAX\u003c/sub\u003e + 3E should be dealt with as storm overflows.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ePermits issued must include necessary conditions such as overflow location, type, weir setting, storage requirements, and aesthetic performance standards. Permits may also contain spill frequency performance targets. The \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e will not normally consider it necessary to apply chemical and bacteriological quality conditions in the permit unless the solution relies upon treatment.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"additional-requirements-for-storm-overflows-discharging-to-coastal-and-estuarine-waters\"\u003e7.2.5 Additional requirements for storm overflows discharging to coastal and estuarine waters\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eFurther control of combined sewage overflows to coastal and estuarine tidal waters is needed to ensure that, where waters are identified under the provisions of the Bathing Water Directive, compliance with the requirements of that directive is not compromised by the adverse effect of such discharges.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt is recognised that there are distinct variations in the nature of receiving coastal and estuarine waters. This publication is therefore designed to take into account local conditions and provide a framework for issuing permits which reflect the local needs and benefits to the environment.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe need to limit the operation of tidal storm overflows and provide emission control of sewage solids through the use of appropriate solids retention techniques is also described.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn general, subject to specified exceptional circumstances, the following requirements will apply as a minimum:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eMinimum retained flow: The sewerage system should be designed so that the storm overflow will not spill until the incoming flow exceeds that calculated from ‘Formula A’, or equivalent. The Formula is to be amended as described in the report of the Technical Committee on Storm Overflows and the Disposal of Storm Sewage (1970) for any separate areas within the sewered catchment.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe paragraphs in relation to the normal minimum design requirement and necessary permit conditions in section 7.2.4, also apply here.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eLocation: The outfall soffit level of all storm overflows must be located below the level of low water mark of mean spring tides (\u003cabbr title=\"mean low water level of springtides\"\u003eMLWS\u003c/abbr\u003e).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhere there are particular local extenuating circumstances which either prevent or render it impractical to locate the outfall in accordance with the minimum requirement, then the following guidance should be applied, appropriate to the receiving water category.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA spill frequency standard should be applied as follows:\u003c/p\u003e\u003ctable\u003e\n  \u003cthead\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"col\"\u003eSoffit level\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"col\"\u003eOperational setting\u003c/th\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n  \u003c/thead\u003e\n  \u003ctbody\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eStorm overflow soffit above \u003cabbr title=\"mean low water level of springtides\"\u003eMLWS\u003c/abbr\u003e but below the level of high water of mean spring tides (\u003cabbr title=\"mean high water level of springtides\"\u003eMHWS\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eSpill frequency should be set between 3 spills per season and 1 spill in every 5 bathing seasons based on local considerations and the actual location of the storm overflow soffit.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eStorm overflow soffit at \u003cabbr title=\"mean high water level of springtides\"\u003eMHWS\u003c/abbr\u003e\n\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eSpill frequency should be limited to 1 spill in every 5 bathing seasons.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eStorm overflow soffit above \u003cabbr title=\"mean high water level of springtides\"\u003eMHWS\u003c/abbr\u003e\n\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eSpill frequency should be limited to 1 spill in every 5 years.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n  \u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor short sea outfalls located within designated bathing waters, these sites will still impact bathing waters, but the operational settings will be determined with reference to the \u003cabbr title=\"Environment Agency\"\u003eEA\u003c/abbr\u003e’s bathing water guidance (2018).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhere the water and sewerage company intends to extend the outfall of the storm overflow some distance offshore of \u003cabbr title=\"mean low water level of springtides\"\u003eMLWS\u003c/abbr\u003e to achieve improved dispersion of the discharge of storm sewage, the following criterion may be adopted:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAchievement of the water quality standards of the Bathing Water Directive should be achieved in not less than 98.2% of the bathing season.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn such circumstances, the water and sewerage company should consider any offshore shellfish waters in their planning and modelling.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe impact criterion should only be used in those circumstances where extensive studies, including field exercises, can be undertaken and the regulatory authority with responsibility for auditing such information provided by the water and sewerage company can be reasonably satisfied with the validity of the assumptions made and the predictions produced.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"categories-of-receiving-water-aesthetic-amenity-and-value\"\u003e7.2.6 Categories of receiving water aesthetic amenity and value\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe categories of amenity use outlined in section 7.3 should be used.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhen assigning the amenity category, account should be taken of the affected receiving waters for a reasonable distance downstream as well as those in the immediate vicinity of the discharge.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"categories-of-receiving-water-aesthetic-amenity-and-value-1\"\u003e7.3 Categories of receiving water aesthetic amenity and value\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eBelow are the categories used to describe the aesthetic amenity and value of receiving waters with examples of criteria used to define its amenity and value.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"high-amenity\"\u003e7.3.1 High amenity\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eInfluences area where bathing and water contact sport (immersion) is regularly practised (such as wind-surfing, sports canoeing).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eReceiving watercourse passes through formal public park.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFormal picnic site.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eDesignated shellfish waters.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eDesignated bathing waters.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWaters designated under the Conservation of Habitats and Species Regulations 2017 as special areas of conservation (\u003cabbr title=\"special areas of conservation\"\u003eSACs\u003c/abbr\u003e).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSites designated under the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands of International Importance especially as Waterfowl Habitat.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"moderate-amenity\"\u003e7.3.2 Moderate amenity\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eBoating on receiving water.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ePopular footpath adjacent to watercourse.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWatercourse passes through housing development or frequently used town centre area (such as a bridge, pedestrian area, or shopping area).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRecreation and contact sport (non-immersion) areas.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt is linked through substantiated reasons for failure of Water Framework Directive water body status classification being less than good.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"low-amenity\"\u003e7.3.3 Low amenity\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eBasic amenity use only.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eCasual riverside access on a limited or infrequent basis, such as a road bridge in a rural area, footpath adjacent to watercourse.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"non-amenity\"\u003e7.3.4 Non-amenity\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eSeldom or never used for amenity purposes.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRemote or inaccessible area.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"footnotes\" role=\"doc-endnotes\"\u003e\n  \u003col\u003e\n    \u003cli id=\"fn:1\"\u003e\n      \u003cp\u003eNatural Resources Wales is the responsible regulatory authority for Wales under the \u003cabbr title=\"Environmental Permitting (England and Wales) Regulations 2016\"\u003eEPR 2016\u003c/abbr\u003e. \u003ca href=\"#fnref:1\" class=\"reversefootnote\" role=\"doc-backlink\" aria-label=\"go to where this is referenced\"\u003e↩\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n    \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003c/ol\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e"
      }
    }
  ]
}

  <div data-module="govspeak" class="gem-c-govspeak gem-c-govspeak--direction-ltr govuk-!-margin-bottom-0">
    
    
        <div class="govspeak"><h2 id="introduction">1. Introduction</h2>

<h3 id="objectives">1.1 Objectives</h3>

<p>The objectives of this publication are to provide advice to the sector on the management and regulation of storm overflows, including:</p>

<ul>
  <li>reflecting the evolution in the understanding of storm overflows legislation and developments in policy since the <a rel="external" href="https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1994/2841/contents">Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations 1994</a> (<abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994)</li>
  <li>providing additional information on how to implement measures identified in the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/storm-overflows-discharge-reduction-plan">storm overflows discharge reduction plan</a> (<abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr>)</li>
</ul>

<p>The intention is to support water and sewerage companies and the regulators in carrying out their responsibilities in relation to storm overflows.</p>

<p>The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (<abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr>) wants to ensure a clear planning framework, to support:</p>

<ul>
  <li>the significant forward investment needed from water and sewerage companies</li>
  <li>a robust oversight and enforcement regime</li>
</ul>

<p>We also want to ensure transparency and accountability, recognising the significant public interest in tackling sewage pollution, and to provide assurance to customers.</p>

<p>Since 1994, understanding of the legal requirements surrounding storm overflows has evolved. There have been updates to:</p>

<ul>
  <li>the interpretation of legal requirements, such as through the Court of Justice of the European Union in European Commission v UK (Re Storm Water Overflows) [2013] 1 CMLR 24</li>
  <li>policy and regulatory tools that contribute to bringing these requirements into effect, for example via:
    <ul>
      <li>the Environment Agency (<abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>)’s storm overflow assessment framework (<abbr title="storm overflow assessment framework">SOAF</abbr>) (first issued in 2018, updated in 2025)</li>
      <li>the Environment Act 2021, which introduced requirements such as the need for the Secretary of State to prepare a <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> and for annual reports on discharges from storm overflows</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>Alongside this, the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr>, first published in 2022 and expanded in 2023, sets out an investment and improvement programme to 2050 with the aim of reducing harm to public health and the environment from storm overflows. The <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> contains 3 headline targets that water and sewerage companies will deliver over the next 25 years.</p>

<p>As the legal and policy landscape has developed, so has technological capability. All storm overflows operated by water and sewerage companies whose areas are wholly or mainly in England are now fitted with event duration monitors (<abbr title="event duration monitors">EDMs</abbr>), allowing water and sewerage companies to report on the frequency and duration of storm overflow discharges in near real time.</p>

<p><abbr title="event duration monitor">EDM</abbr> data provides greater insight into the operation of storm overflows than ever before. It should be utilised by water and sewerage companies and regulators to inform daily operation, maintenance of and required upgrades to the sewerage system.</p>

<p>Monitoring data can also be used to help identify possible compliance issues with legal requirements. This publication seeks to provide greater clarity on how monitoring data may be used to inform investigations and storm overflow improvements.</p>

<p>On 23 October 2024, the UK and Welsh governments launched an independent commission to recommend reforms to reset the water sector regulatory system. The commission aims to build consensus for a resilient and innovative water sector and a robust regulatory framework that will:</p>

<ul>
  <li>deliver long-term benefits</li>
  <li>restore rivers, lakes and seas to good health</li>
  <li>provide a reliable and efficient water supply in a changing climate</li>
  <li>ultimately, serve both customers and the environment</li>
</ul>

<p>Once the commission has made recommendations, both governments will respond and consult on proposals, including potential legislation.</p>

<h3 id="scope-and-how-we-expect-this-publication-to-be-used">1.2 Scope and how we expect this publication to be used</h3>

<p>This publication is intended to provide information and strategic guidance for the management and regulation of storm overflows, from the point of assessment to the delivery of improvements and enforcement of regulatory requirements.</p>

<p>This document does not impose any new legal requirements on regulators or water and sewerage companies. It is instead restating and clarifying the current position on storm overflows regulation and management, including to support preparations for future price reviews.</p>

<h4 id="scope">1.2.1 Scope</h4>

<p>This publication applies to water and sewerage companies and regulators in respect of storm overflows operated by water and sewerage companies whose area is wholly or mainly in England. In this context, ‘regulators’ refers to Ofwat or the Environment Agency (<abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>). </p>

<p>There are approximately 14,500 storm overflows in England, both on the network and at wastewater treatment works. This publication also applies to storm overflows at pumping stations, which serve combined systems (both rainfall runoff and foul flow). They act as hydraulic control for flows in excess of the designed pump rate to treatment.</p>

<p>It does not apply to other types of assets or overflows including emergency overflows, due to the different applications of these assets and the different regulatory schemes which apply to these.</p>

<h4 id="areas-of-focus">1.2.2 Areas of focus</h4>

<p>This document opens with a focus on advancements in relation to the monitoring of storm overflows, and how resultant data can be used to support the delivery of storm overflow improvements and compliance with legal and policy requirements.</p>

<p>It then provides a summary of the legislative and policy requirements for storm overflows, under the <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994 and the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr>. It sets out how the ‘best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs’ (<abbr title="best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs">BTKNEEC</abbr>) test should be implemented in practice, taking into account relevant case law and developments, and provides further detail on how the targets under the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> should be met.</p>

<p>Moving onto implementation, the document explains how investigations should be carried out, and how improvements should be delivered. This section of the document seeks to provide advice for regulators in carrying out their statutory duties, as well as considerations for water and sewerage companies to support them in planning and delivering the substantial forward investment programme required.</p>

<p>The document then summarises <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr>, the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> and Ofwat’s enforcement responsibilities.</p>

<p>Finally, this document updates elements of previous <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> guidance on storm overflows. Draft guidance on the <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994 was issued to dischargers and regulators in July 1997 (the 1997 guidance). It was intended as a working document for dischargers and regulators on the implementation and interpretation of the <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994. Information in respect of storm overflows was largely found in Annex 8 of the 1997 guidance, which covered:</p>

<ul>
  <li>the definition of unsatisfactory overflows</li>
  <li>consenting for satisfactory and unsatisfactory overflows</li>
  <li>the procedure for reviewing overflows to freshwaters and discharges into coastal waters and estuaries</li>
</ul>

<p>With the exception of a limited update in 2009, the 1997 guidance has not been revised since it was published. This document now supersedes parts of Annex 3 and all of Annex 8 for storm overflows operated by water and sewerage companies whose area is wholly or mainly in England (but not for storm overflows operated by water and sewerage companies whose area is wholly or mainly in Wales). Those parts of the 1997 guidance will be withdrawn and replaced by Section 7 of this document. The rest of the 1997 guidance is still applicable.</p>

<p>Section 7 has been provided by the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> and is intended as a guideline for water and sewerage companies. Companies should also refer to the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>’s latest guidance (including the storm overflow assessment framework (<abbr title="storm overflow assessment framework">SOAF</abbr>) version 2) and relevant legal requirements.</p>

<p>This document signposts other technical and regulatory guidance where appropriate, such as the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>’s <abbr title="storm overflow assessment framework">SOAF</abbr> version 2. The <abbr title="storm overflow assessment framework">SOAF</abbr> version 2 sets out technical details and processes for prioritising the investigation and improvement of individual assets. It should be read in conjunction with:</p>

<ul>
  <li>the <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994</li>
  <li>the requirement to provide and maintain the sewerage network under section 94 of the Water Industry Act 1991 (<abbr title="Water Industry Act 1991">WIA 1991</abbr>)</li>
</ul>
