<h4 id="how-this-publication-should-be-used">1.2.3 How this publication should be used</h4>

<p>This publication is non-statutory and is not intended to replace or amend existing legislative requirements. In addition, while every effort has been made to ensure that explanations included in this document are accurate, only the courts can give authoritative interpretation of the law.</p>

<p>There may also be legal obligations to which this document does not refer, but which must be complied with. Water and sewerage companies should seek legal advice and consult with regulators where they are unclear about the scope and effect of applicable legislation.</p>

<p>It is ultimately water and sewerage companies’ responsibility to ensure that they comply with their legal requirements.</p>

<p>This publication will be kept under review and updated as needed, including in advance of <abbr title="2029 price review">PR29</abbr> (2030 to 2035).</p>

<h2 id="monitoring-and-advancements-in-data">2. Monitoring and advancements in data</h2>

<p>This section reflects key developments in monitoring and data since the <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994. It does not provide an exhaustive list of storm overflow monitoring requirements.</p>

<h3 id="event-duration-monitoring">2.1 Event duration monitoring</h3>

<p>All storm overflows now have monitors installed recording the frequency and duration of their operation. The programme to install event duration monitors (<abbr title="event duration monitors">EDMs</abbr>) on storm overflows was completed in December 2023.</p>

<p>The <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> will continue to oversee <abbr title="event duration monitor">EDM</abbr> installation, operation and reporting by way of their functions under the Environmental Permitting (England and Wales) Regulations 2016 (the <abbr title="Environmental Permitting (England and Wales) Regulations 2016">EPR 2016</abbr>).</p>

<p>Water and sewerage companies should refer to industry best practice on <abbr title="event duration monitors">EDMs</abbr>. This includes the Chartered Institution of Water and Environmental Management (<abbr title="Chartered Institution of Water and Environmental Management">CIWEM</abbr>) <a rel="external" href="https://www.ciwem.org/assets/uploads/CIWEM_UDG_EDM_Good_Practice_Guide_2021_final.pdf">Event Duration Monitoring Good Practice Guide</a>. They should ensure that monitors are appropriately accredited and perform in line with <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> and Ofwat guidance.</p>

<h4 id="annual-edm-reporting">2.1.1 Annual <abbr title="event duration monitor">EDM</abbr> reporting</h4>

<p>The <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> has a duty under section 141D of the <abbr title="Water Industry Act 1991">WIA 1991</abbr> (inserted by the Environment Act 2021) to publish an annual summary of measured <abbr title="event duration monitor">EDM</abbr> data by the end of March each year for the preceding calendar year.</p>

<p>Water and sewerage companies should present <abbr title="event duration monitor">EDM</abbr> data for annual reporting and compliance purposes using the 12 hour and 24 hour block spill counting method, as described in section 3.2 of this document. Information from <abbr title="event duration monitors">EDMs</abbr> regarding start and stop times of a discharge should be maintained by water and sewerage companies and made available to regulators on request.</p>

<p>For storm overflows determined as having potential to impact on designated bathing waters, water and sewerage companies should provide a report to the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> on <abbr title="event duration monitor">EDM</abbr> and storm overflow performance for the period of the bathing season (May to September).</p>

<h4 id="near-real-time-reporting-of-edm-data">2.1.2 Near real time reporting of <abbr title="event duration monitor">EDM</abbr> data</h4>

<p>Since 1 January 2025, water and sewerage companies have been required to publish storm overflow data in near real time, pursuant to the requirement introduced by section 81 of the Environment Act 2021.</p>

<p>That section introduced a duty for water and sewerage companies to publish information on when a storm overflow discharge:</p>

<ul>
  <li>begins and the location of the storm overflow (within an hour of the discharge beginning)</li>
  <li>ends (within an hour of the discharge ending)</li>
</ul>

<p>This information should be published in a way which is readily accessible and understandable to the public.</p>

<p>Ofwat, is responsible for overseeing compliance with this duty. Ofwat’s 2024 price review (<abbr title="2024 price review">PR24</abbr>) <a rel="external" href="https://www.ofwat.gov.uk/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/Storm-overflows-PC-definition.pdf">common performance commitments for storm overflows</a> will incentivise water and sewerage companies to maintain <abbr title="event duration monitors">EDMs</abbr> and record discharges. The performance measure calculation takes monitored spills and unmonitored storm overflows into consideration.</p>

<h4 id="use-of-edm-data-for-regulatory-purposes">2.1.3 Use of <abbr title="event duration monitor">EDM</abbr> data for regulatory purposes</h4>

<p>The <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> will use <abbr title="event duration monitor">EDM</abbr> data to:</p>

<ul>
  <li>inform their duties in the regulation of storm overflows</li>
  <li>assess delivery against targets, including those laid out in the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr>
</li>
</ul>

<p>Ofwat will utilise <abbr title="event duration monitor">EDM</abbr> data to inform their:</p>

<ul>
  <li>enforcement duties in the regulation of storm overflows</li>
  <li>policy and decisions in relation to water and sewerage companies’ investment programmes, to ensure their sewerage assets are and continue to be built and operated to meet their environmental obligations</li>
</ul>

<p>The <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> and Ofwat will continue to review any technological advancements in monitoring. Where appropriate, advancements may inform specific <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> permit conditions, which may result in enhanced obligations for water and sewerage companies to implement additional data monitoring requirements. Examples of possible advancements include:</p>

<ul>
  <li>new monitoring intervals</li>
  <li>reporting frequencies</li>
  <li>requirements for telemetry</li>
  <li>assurance and certification schemes</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="continuous-water-quality-monitoring-of-the-receiving-water-environment">2.2 Continuous water quality monitoring of the receiving water environment</h3>

<p>Water and sewerage companies are beginning to install continuous water quality monitoring (<abbr title="continuous water quality monitoring">CWQM</abbr>) monitors in the <abbr title="2024 price review">PR24</abbr> period (2025 to 2030), focusing on high priority assets.</p>

<p>Water quality metrics measured by the <abbr title="continuous water quality monitoring">CWQM</abbr> programme are specifically aligned to those required to assess receiving water quality against the urban pollution management (<abbr title="urban pollution management">UPM</abbr>) fundamental intermittent standards (<abbr title="fundamental intermittent standards">FIS</abbr>) for levels of ammonia, dissolved oxygen, temperatures, pH values and turbidity.</p>

<p>Data collected in accordance with the <abbr title="continuous water quality monitoring">CWQM</abbr> programme will be used by regulators and water and sewerage companies to inform the development of schemes to deliver the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> requirements, particularly the ecological target (see section 3.2).</p>

<p>The data will also support:</p>

<ul>
  <li>the successful delivery of improvement schemes to meet storm overflow legal requirements and targets</li>
  <li>
<abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> river basin planning work in assessing reasons for not achieving good status (<abbr title="reasons for not achieving good status">RNAGS</abbr>)</li>
</ul>

<p>The regulators will also use this data alongside <abbr title="event duration monitor">EDM</abbr> data to inform their policy and enforcement activities, for example to check for permit breaches.</p>

<h2 id="basis-for-storm-overflow-improvements">3. Basis for storm overflow improvements</h2>

<h3 id="legal-requirements">3.1 Legal requirements</h3>

<p>This section outlines key legal requirements that apply to the use and maintenance of storm overflows, and to associated enforcement action.</p>

<p>Of central importance here are the Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations 1994 (‘<abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr>’), which include (among other things) requirements for the design and operation of sewers, treatment works and storm overflows, whilst also setting out the treatment standards to be applied.</p>

<p>This section should not be treated as an exhaustive list of the applicable legal requirements in this area, and water and sewerage companies should continue to refer to relevant legislation and case law. Regulators can also be consulted for advice.</p>

<h4 id="statutory-requirements">3.1.1 Statutory requirements</h4>

<p>Section 94 of the Water Industry Act 1991 (<abbr title="Water Industry Act 1991">WIA 1991</abbr>) imposes a duty on water and sewerage companies to provide, improve and extend such a system of public sewers, and so to cleanse and maintain those sewers, as to ensure that the area is and continues to be effectually drained.</p>

<p>Companies are also required to make provision for the emptying of those sewers and such further provision as is necessary from time to time for effectually dealing with (by means of sewage disposal or otherwise) the contents of those sewers.</p>

<p>The <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994 transposed the Urban Waste Water Treatment Directive (the <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment Directive">UWWTD</abbr>) with respect to England and Wales. They supplement section 94 of the <abbr title="Water Industry Act 1991">WIA 1991</abbr>.</p>

<p>Together, the <abbr title="Water Industry Act 1991">WIA 1991</abbr> and the <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994 impose obligations on water and sewerage companies, the Secretary of State, and regulators. In this context, ‘regulators’ refers to Ofwat, and the applicable of the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> or Natural Resources Wales.</p>

<p>Where obligations are not complied with, regulators can take enforcement action, relying on powers conferred under the <abbr title="Water Industry Act 1991">WIA 1991</abbr> or the <abbr title="Environmental Permitting (England and Wales) Regulations 2016">EPR 2016</abbr>.</p>

<h4 id="duties-on-water-and-sewerage-companies">3.1.2 Duties on water and sewerage companies</h4>

<p>Regulation 4 of the <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994 sets out mandatory requirements for water and sewerage companies when carrying out their duties to provide and maintain adequate sewerage systems under section 94 of the <abbr title="Water Industry Act 1991">WIA 1991</abbr>.</p>

<p>Regulation 4 contains obligations in respect of both collecting systems and treatment plants. Key obligations include that companies must:</p>

<p>1. Ensure collecting systems meet the requirements set out in Schedule 2 (regulation 4(2)). Paragraph 2 of Schedule 2 provides that collecting systems should be designed, constructed and maintained in accordance with the ‘best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs’ (<abbr title="best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs">BTKNEEC</abbr>) test, particularly in relation to the:</p>

<ul>
  <li>volume and characteristics of urban waste water</li>
  <li>prevention of leaks</li>
  <li>limitation of pollution of receiving waters due to storm water overflows</li>
</ul>

<p>To note, the Court of Justice of the European Union (<abbr title="Court of Justice of the European Union">CJEU</abbr>) clarified at [63] of European Commission v UK (Re Storm Water Overflows) [2013] 1 CMLR 24 that the <abbr title="best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs">BTKNEEC</abbr> test extends to treatment plants as well as collecting systems.</p>

<p>2. Ensure that treatment plants are designed (account being taken of seasonal variations of the load), constructed, operated and maintained, to ensure sufficient performance under all normal local climatic conditions (regulation 4(4)(a)).</p>

<p>3. Ensure disposal routes for treated waste water and sludge minimise adverse effects on the environment (regulation 4(4)(c)).</p>

<p>The term collecting system refers to a system of sewers for collecting and conducting urban waste water.</p>

<p>Companies are responsible for ensuring compliance with the relevant legal requirements. Where necessary, companies should liaise with regulators regarding any questions they may have on requirements related to specific assets or permit conditions. This includes liaising with the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> to ensure assets and permits remain compliant with the obligations under the <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr>. Companies must comply with permit conditions and ensure that all details contained on the permit are accurate.</p>

<h4 id="duties-on-regulators">3.1.3 Duties on regulators</h4>

<p>Regulation 6 of the <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994 imposes a duty on the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> when exercising their functions under the <abbr title="Environmental Permitting (England and Wales) Regulations 2016">EPR 2016</abbr> (such as in granting, varying or revoking environmental permits), to secure ‘the limitation of pollution of receiving waters due to storm overflows’ in respect of discharges from collecting systems and treatment plants (regulation 6(2)(c)).<sup id="fnref:1"><a href="#fn:1" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 1]</a></sup></p>

<p>The <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> should review and, where appropriate, vary permit conditions in such a way as to reflect <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> and other legislative requirements (see relevant <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> permitting guidance).</p>

<p>Ofwat also has responsibility for enforcing regulation 4 <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994, as it supplements the duty in section 94 <abbr title="Water Industry Act 1991">WIA 1991</abbr> which Ofwat also enforces.</p>

<h4 id="case-law-and-the-btkneec-test">3.1.4 Case law and the <abbr title="best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs">BTKNEEC</abbr> test</h4>

<p>The requirements under the <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994 were considered by the Court of Justice of the European Union (<abbr title="Court of Justice of the European Union">CJEU</abbr>) in European Commission v UK (Re Storm Water Overflows) [2013] 1 CMLR 24. The <abbr title="Court of Justice of the European Union">CJEU</abbr>’s findings were summarised by the High Court at [63]-[70] of R (on the application of WildFish Conservation and Marine Conservation Society and others) v Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (‘WildFish’) [2023] EHWC 2285 (Admin).</p>

<p>The <abbr title="Court of Justice of the European Union">CJEU</abbr> identified that:</p>

<ul>
  <li>all urban waste water must be collected and treated under usual climatic and seasonal conditions</li>
  <li>a failure to treat urban waste water can only be tolerated where the circumstances are ‘out of the ordinary’</li>
</ul>

<p>At the same time, the <abbr title="Court of Justice of the European Union">CJEU</abbr> acknowledged footnote 1 to Annexes 1(A) and 1(B) of the <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment Directive">UWWTD</abbr>, which recognises that it is not possible in practice to construct collecting systems and treatment plants so that all waste water is capable of being treated. Such situations can be tolerated in “situations such as unusually heavy rainfall”, which the <abbr title="Court of Justice of the European Union">CJEU</abbr> characterised as “exceptional situations” or “exceptional circumstances”.</p>

<p>However, in those situations the state must decide on “measures to limit pollution from storm water overflows”. As per the <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment Directive">UWWTD</abbr> footnote, such measures could be based on dilution rates or capacity in relation to dry weather flow, or could specify a certain acceptable number of overflows per year.</p>

<p>In practice, this means that discharges of untreated waste water from collecting systems and treatment plants should only occur in exceptional circumstances, unless remedial intervention would not satisfy the <abbr title="best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs">BTKNEEC</abbr> test.</p>

<p>Per the summary of the <abbr title="Court of Justice of the European Union">CJEU</abbr>’s findings in WildFish, the <abbr title="best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs">BTKNEEC</abbr> test involves weighing the best technology and its estimated costs against the benefits, or avoidance of harm, that a more effective water collection or treatment system may provide.</p>

<p>This involves taking into account the effects of discharges of untreated waste on the environment to see whether the costs that must be incurred or the works necessary to treat all waste water, would be proportionate to the environmental benefit that would result.</p>

<p>Storm overflow discharges should therefore be assessed via the following two-stage test:</p>

<ol>
  <li>Is the storm overflow discharging outside of ‘exceptional circumstances’?</li>
  <li>If the discharge is not due to exceptional circumstances, is there a solution to improve the storm overflow which satisfies the <abbr title="best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs">BTKNEEC</abbr> test?</li>
</ol>

<p>The two-stage test should be applied on a case-by-case basis.</p>

<p>Regulators and water and sewerage companies are expected to have regard to any relevant updates in case law on storm overflows when exercising their legal obligations.</p>

<h4 id="implementation-of-the-two-stage-test">3.1.5 Implementation of the two-stage test</h4>

<p>The <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>’s <abbr title="storm overflow assessment framework">SOAF</abbr> version 2 (when published), and <a rel="external" href="https://www.water.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/Storm-Overflow-Benefits-Vaulation-Final-Practitioners-Guide.pdf">guidance on valuing the benefits of storm discharge improvements</a> (<abbr title="cost-benefit analysis">CBA</abbr> process and Practitioners’ Guide are subject to review ahead of updating in 2025) provide a framework to support water and sewerage companies in identifying storm overflows which need remediation. This includes setting out guidance for how companies should carry out the <abbr title="best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs">BTKNEEC</abbr> test.</p>

<p><abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> expects the two-stage test to be applied in a robust and consistent manner across all storm overflows and water and sewerage companies.</p>

<p>Regulators will set an appropriate benefit cost ratio (<abbr title="benefit cost ratio">BCR</abbr>) to determine excessive cost. The <abbr title="benefit cost ratio">BCR</abbr> will be set and updated according to best practice and best available evidence.</p>

<p>Water and sewerage companies must report to the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> after both stages of the two-stage test and provide all <abbr title="storm overflow assessment framework">SOAF</abbr> outcomes to the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>, including where there is no solution which satisfies the <abbr title="best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs">BTKNEEC</abbr> test, as outlined in the <abbr title="storm overflow assessment framework">SOAF</abbr> version 2.</p>

<p>In practice, water and sewerage companies provide this information to the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> via their annual <abbr title="event duration monitor">EDM</abbr> returns. The <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> verifies this information and makes it available to Ofwat alongside its publication.    </p>

<p>The <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> will develop a specific reporting mechanism for more frequent updates on the progress of <abbr title="storm overflow assessment framework">SOAF</abbr> investigations and improvements. They will share this data as appropriate with other regulators.</p>

<p>Water and sewerage companies should keep their <abbr title="best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs">BTKNEEC</abbr> assessments up to date and review them periodically, at least every 5 years. The depth of a review will generally depend on what has changed since the previous assessment and should be determined by water and sewerage companies on a case-by-case basis. Factors that may highlight the need for a review, and will help determine the scope of a review, include:</p>

<ul>
  <li>change in spill frequency or duration</li>
  <li>additional designations (such as a new bathing water site)</li>
  <li>other changes in the catchment</li>
  <li>risk or change identified in the drainage and wastewater management plan (<abbr title="drainage and wastewater management plan">DWMP</abbr>)</li>
  <li>new technology is available</li>
  <li>new information on benefits or costs</li>
</ul>

<p>Keeping <abbr title="best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs">BTKNEEC</abbr> tests up to date should ensure that:</p>

<ul>
  <li>the design, build, operation and maintenance of each asset remains consistent with <abbr title="best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs">BTKNEEC</abbr> as knowledge develops</li>
  <li>the changing costs and benefits at each site are reflected as they evolve</li>
  <li>the network is maintained, improved and extended as needed</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="unusually-heavy-rainfall-events">3.1.6 Unusually heavy rainfall events</h4>

<p>As set out above, ‘unusually heavy rainfall’ was characterised as an ‘exceptional circumstance’ by the <abbr title="Court of Justice of the European Union">CJEU</abbr> in the ‘UK’ case. The <abbr title="storm overflow assessment framework">SOAF</abbr> version 2 sets out a methodology for identifying ‘unusually heavy’ rainfall events for the purpose of prioritising investigations to assets which spill frequently in more typical years.</p>

<h3 id="policy--storm-overflows-discharge-reduction-plan">3.2 Policy – storm overflows discharge reduction plan</h3>

<p>This section provides further information on the implementation of the targets contained in the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr>. It does not add to the requirements on water and sewerage companies outlined in the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> but provides additional guidance on delivery against the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr>’s targets.</p>

<p>The <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr>, published in accordance with section 141A of the <abbr title="Water Industry Act 1991">WIA 1991</abbr>, set 3 ambitious targets for water and sewerage companies:</p>

<ul>
  <li>an ecological target and public health target (with these being the main drivers for improvement)</li>
  <li>a rainfall target (interpreted as a maximum of 10 recorded spills on average per year as reported in the statutory <abbr title="event duration monitor">EDM</abbr> return)</li>
</ul>

<p>The targets in the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> were augmented by the 2023 update to the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr>, which included a greater spread of high priority sites. High priority sites are defined in the ‘Ecological target’ sub-section (3.2.2).</p>

<p>The <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> aims to increase ambition on reducing the harm caused by storm overflows. It goes further than the <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994 in most circumstances because improvements to meet its targets are not subject to a cost-benefit style assessment.</p>

<p>While the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> has a statutory basis by virtue of its being required by the amendments made to the <abbr title="Water Industry Act 1991">WIA 1991</abbr> by the Environment Act 2021, the contents of the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> are not legally binding. Water and sewerage companies have, however, committed to delivering against these targets. Compliance with the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> targets at an asset level will be implemented by way of environmental permits.</p>

<p>An update on delivery against the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> targets will be published in <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr>’s 2025 progress report, as required by the Environment Act 2021.</p>

<h4 id="implementation-of-the-targets">3.2.1 Implementation of the targets</h4>

<p>Water and sewerage companies should use the technologies, data and modelling available to them to ensure their sewer networks are operated to meet their legal obligations and the targets set out in the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr>. Considerations that apply to particular <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> targets are outlined in sections 3.2.2 to 3.2.4.</p>

<p>There are also some general considerations applicable to achievement of all of the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> targets, which are detailed in this section.</p>

<p>These considerations have been developed in conjunction with the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>, as the expert organisation responsible for the regulatory implementation of the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr>.</p>

<h5 id="length-of-period-to-assess-average-spill-performance">3.2.1.1 Length of period to assess average spill performance</h5>

<p>The <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> spill frequency targets for storm overflows (ecological, bathing and rainfall targets) are defined as an average over 10 consecutive years.</p>

<p>It is recognised that a 10-year assessment requires significant time to determine permit compliance and therefore, to secure early identification of underperforming storm overflows, the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> may use a shorter-term regulatory compliance assessment.</p>

<h5 id="spill-counting-methodology">3.2.1.2 Spill counting methodology</h5>

<p>There is a distinction between ‘discharges’ and ‘spills’.</p>

<p>When a signal from an <abbr title="event duration monitor">EDM</abbr> device is verified, this means that a storm overflow discharge has taken place. For the purposes of <abbr title="event duration monitor">EDM</abbr> on storm overflows that discharge to the environment, spills (or spill count) is the discharge count with the 12 and 24 hour block spill counting methodology applied.</p>

<p>Further detail on how this counting methodology works in practice, including when assessing against spill targets, can be found in the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>’s <abbr title="storm overflow assessment framework">SOAF</abbr> version 2.</p>

<h5 id="counting-and-discounting-spills">3.2.1.2 Counting and discounting spills</h5>

<p>When assessing against spill targets, the 12 and 24 hour block spill count of the individual assets should be assessed in isolation against the applicable <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> target. Spills from multiple discharges into a common receiving water should not be aggregated together when assessing against a spill count threshold. </p>

<p>If assessing against an ecological or environmental quality standard in the receiving waters, such as a shellfish water, then the combined effects of multiple storm overflows will be assessed.</p>

<p>No discharges or ‘calculated spills’ (which are spills counted using the 12 and 24 hour block spill count method) shall be discounted or removed from the counting process or spill count on the basis of small volume being considered likely to have no or small impact on the receiving waters.</p>

<h5 id="design-horizons-for-improvement-schemes">3.2.1.3 Design horizons for improvement schemes</h5>

<p>When designing spill performance against a spill target, it is recommended that a rainfall series of up to 25 years is used, due to the annual variability of rainfall.</p>

<p>Recognising that this will not always be possible, a minimum of 10 years’ data should be assessed.</p>

<p>If insufficient historical rainfall is available, a synthetic rainfall series will need to be developed. <a rel="external" href="https://www.ciwem.org/assets/pdf/Special%20Interest%20Groups/Urban%20Drainage%20Group/CIWEM-UDG-Rainfall-Guide-2016.pdf">The <abbr title="Chartered Institution of Water and Environmental Management">CIWEM</abbr> Rainfall Modelling Guide</a> should be followed.</p>

<p>The rainfall series should be typical over the duration of the series and wet or exceptionally wet years should not be removed.</p>

<h5 id="using-sewer-hydraulic-models-to-design-against-spill-targets">3.2.1.4 Using sewer hydraulic models to design against spill targets</h5>

<p>Storm overflow improvements to meet spill frequency targets should make use of sewer hydraulic modelling.</p>

<p>Models should be built, verified, applied and maintained in accordance with the <a rel="external" href="https://www.ciwem.org/assets/pdf/Special%20Interest%20Groups/Urban%20Drainage%20Group/Code%20of%20Practice%20for%20the%20Hydraulic%20Modelling%20of%20Ur.pdf"><abbr title="Chartered Institution of Water and Environmental Management">CIWEM</abbr> Code of Practice for the Hydraulic Modelling of Urban Drainage Systems</a>.</p>

<h5 id="strategic-planning-and-allowing-for-climate-change-and-other-pressures-on-sewerage-in-the-design">3.2.1.5 Strategic planning and allowing for climate change and other pressures on sewerage in the design</h5>

<p>Capacity pressures on sewerage systems include climate change (rainfall), population growth and urban creep, as well as ageing assets.</p>

<p>Water and sewerage companies should design their storm overflow improvements using planning horizons over the longer term (to 25 years) to address complex environmental issues and account for a range of future climate change scenarios and other pressures. </p>

<p>It is the water and sewerage companies’ responsibility to achieve and maintain storm overflow performance against the spill frequency targets. Failure to do so could result in permit non-compliance.</p>

<p>Water and sewerage companies should manage the current and future risks to and demands of their drainage and sewerage systems through their <abbr title="drainage and wastewater management plans">DWMPs</abbr>, updated every 5 years and reviewed every year. These plans are required under section 94A of the <abbr title="Water Industry Act 1991">WIA 1991</abbr> (inserted by section 79 of the Environment Act 2021).</p>

<p>Preparing, publishing and maintaining <abbr title="drainage and wastewater management plans">DWMPs</abbr> became a statutory requirement for water and sewerage companies from September 2024. Companies are expected to publish <abbr title="drainage and wastewater management plans">DWMPs</abbr> ahead of <abbr title="2029 price review">PR29</abbr>, after which statutory annual reviews will commence.</p>

<h5 id="assessing-performance-against-the-average-spill-targets">3.2.1.6 Assessing performance against the average spill targets</h5>

<p>When assessing spill performance against design targets, the spill performance should be assessed as an average over 10 years. This ensures equivalence against the design target of using a minimum of 10 years’ rainfall to design the storm overflow performance.</p>

<h5 id="assessing-compliance">3.2.1.7 Assessing compliance</h5>

<p>The <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> will protect the spill performance of storm overflow improvement schemes, and the performance of storm overflows which already meet design targets, through spill limit conditions within permits issued under the <abbr title="Environmental Permitting (England and Wales) Regulations 2016">EPR 2016</abbr>.</p>

<p>Non-compliance with limits in permit conditions could result in water and sewerage company investigations and enforcement action.</p>

<h4 id="ecological-target">3.2.2 Ecological target</h4>

<p>The <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> sets out that water and sewerage companies will only be permitted to discharge from a storm overflow where they can demonstrate that there is no local adverse ecological impact, by the deadlines set out in section 3.2.2.1.</p>

<p>This target will ensure that no water body in England fails to achieve good ecological status due to storm overflow discharges. Good ecological status is described in the Water Framework Directive 2000/60/EC (<abbr title="Water Framework Directive">WFD</abbr>), Annex V, 1.2, table 1.2, as follows:</p>

<p>“The values of the biological quality elements for the surface water body type show low levels of distortion resulting from human activity, but deviate only slightly from those normally associated with the surface water body type under undisturbed conditions.”</p>

<h5 id="timelines-for-the-ecological-target">3.2.2.1 Timelines for the ecological target</h5>

<p>Water and sewerage companies will only be permitted to discharge from a storm overflow where they can demonstrate that there is no adverse ecological impact by the following target dates:</p>

<ul>
  <li>2035 for at least 75% of storm overflows discharging into or near ‘high priority sites’</li>
  <li>2045 for all overflows discharging into or near ‘high priority sites’</li>
  <li>2050 for all remaining storm overflows</li>
</ul>

<p>The timeframes for improvements are also dependent on the sensitivities of the receiving waters and any known impacts, such as to bathing waters and ecological ‘high priority sites’.</p>

<h5 id="definition-of-ecological-high-priority-sites">3.2.2.2 Definition of ecological ‘high priority sites’</h5>

<p>In the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr>, ‘high priority sites’ are defined as:</p>

<ul>
  <li>sites of special scientific interest (<abbr title="sites of special scientific interest">SSSIs</abbr>)</li>
  <li>special areas of conservation (<abbr title="special areas of conservation">SACs</abbr>)</li>
  <li>special protected areas (<abbr title="special protection areas">SPAs</abbr>)</li>
  <li>Ramsar sites – wetlands of international importance designated under the Ramsar Convention</li>
  <li>chalk streams</li>
  <li>
<abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994 sensitive areas</li>
  <li>marine conservation zones (<abbr title="marine conservation zones">MCZs</abbr>)</li>
  <li>waters currently failing ecological standards due to storm overflows</li>
  <li>shellfish water protected areas</li>
</ul>

<h5 id="assessing-whether-a-storm-overflow-qualifies-for-the-2035-and-2045-sodrp-targets">3.2.2.3 Assessing whether a storm overflow qualifies for the 2035 and 2045 <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> targets</h5>

<p>The <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> has provided the criteria in this section. These identify whether discharges into, or within a certain distance of, any of the ‘high priority sites’ listed would typically qualify for the associated 2035 and 2045 <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> targets.</p>

<p>Impact modelling cannot be used to prevent a storm overflow site from qualifying as a ‘high priority site’ under the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr>.</p>

<p>Any questions regarding specific assets should be directed to the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>.</p>

<h6 id="criteria-for-high-priority-sites-for-the-ecological-target">Criteria for ‘high priority sites’ for the ecological target</h6>

<p>A storm overflow qualifies as a ‘high priority site’ under the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> if it discharges:</p>

<ul>
  <li>into or within 50m (inland) or 1km (transitional and coastal waters) of an <abbr title="site of special scientific interest">SSSI</abbr> water feature – regardless of whether the water body has favourable or unfavourable status</li>
  <li>into or within 50m (inland) or 1km (transitional and coastal waters) of an <abbr title="special area of conservation">SAC</abbr>, <abbr title="special protection area">SPA</abbr> or Ramsar water feature – regardless of whether the water body has favourable or unfavourable status</li>
  <li>into or within 50m (inland) or 1km (transitional and coastal waters) of a chalk stream</li>
  <li>into or within 1km from the hydraulic continuity of an <abbr title="marine conservation zone">MCZ</abbr>
</li>
</ul>

<h6 id="waters-currently-failing-ecological-standards-due-to-storm-overflows">Waters currently failing ecological standards due to storm overflows</h6>

<p>The <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> requires water and sewerage companies to demonstrate that their storm overflows are having no adverse ecological impact.</p>

<p>To identify sites which are having an adverse impact, water and sewerage companies should refer to the river basin planning ‘reasons for not achieving good status’ (<abbr title="reasons for not achieving good status">RNAGS</abbr>) category. This is made up of <abbr title="reasons for not achieving good status">RNAGS</abbr> and the most recent <abbr title="storm overflow assessment framework">SOAF</abbr> (version 1 or version 2) environmental impact assessments.</p>

<p>Storm overflows should be prioritised to meet the 2035 and 2045 targets if:</p>

<ul>
  <li>an assessment finds that storm overflow discharges are a confirmed or probable ‘reason for not achieving good status’</li>
  <li>an assessment finds that there is an environmental impact through Stage 2 of the <abbr title="storm overflow assessment framework">SOAF</abbr> version 2</li>
</ul>

<h6 id="shellfish-water-protected-areas">Shellfish water protected areas</h6>

<p>A storm overflow qualifies as a high priority site under the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> in relation to ‘designated shellfish waters’, if the discharge is into, or within 1km of hydraulic continuity of, a designated shellfish water.</p>

<h6 id="ecological-standard-for-inland-waters">Ecological standard for inland waters</h6>

<p>Inland waters or freshwaters are defined as those upstream of the tidal limit in estuaries.</p>

<p>‘No local adverse ecological impact’ means achieving the <a rel="external" href="https://fwr.org/publication/urban-pollution-manual-upm/">Urban Pollution Manual (fwr.org)</a> fundamental intermittent standards (<abbr title="fundamental intermittent standards">FIS</abbr>) and 99 percentile standards downstream of the storm overflow discharge point. The <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>’s <abbr title="storm overflow assessment framework">SOAF</abbr> version 2 contains more information on using the <abbr title="fundamental intermittent standards">FIS</abbr> and 99 percentile standards to determine impact.</p>

<p>Achievement of urban pollution management (<abbr title="urban pollution management">UPM</abbr>) <abbr title="fundamental intermittent standards">FIS</abbr> and 99 percentile standards is considered sufficient to prevent harm that would cause a water body to not achieve good ecological status resulting from storm overflow impact. Macroinvertebrate monitoring may be considered in some circumstances to support water quality modelling results. Further detail is set out in <abbr title="storm overflow assessment framework">SOAF</abbr> version 2.</p>

<p>If a storm overflow is resulting in these standards being breached, improvements should be secured in line with the timeframes set out in the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr>.</p>

<h6 id="applying-the-upm-framework-to-inland-waters">Applying the <abbr title="urban pollution management">UPM</abbr> framework to inland waters</h6>

<p>All work affecting storm overflows should be planned using the <abbr title="urban pollution management">UPM</abbr> procedure outlined in <a rel="external" href="https://fwr.org/publication/urban-pollution-manual-upm/">section 3 of the Urban Pollution Manual</a>. The <abbr title="urban pollution management">UPM</abbr> procedure is used to ensure that wastewater discharges from sewer and sewage treatment systems in wet weather meet the ecological requirements of the receiving water in a cost-effective way.</p>

<p>The water sector’s good practice guides such as the <a rel="external" href="https://www.ciwem.org/special-interest-groups/urban-drainage-group">guidance notes and codes of practice</a> published by the <abbr title="Chartered Institution of Water and Environmental Management">CIWEM</abbr> Urban Drainage Group, should be used to inform the detail of how to build, verify and apply <abbr title="urban pollution management">UPM</abbr> modelling techniques.</p>

<h6 id="ecological-standards-for-coastal-and-estuarine-waters">Ecological standards for coastal and estuarine waters</h6>

<p>Due to the technical challenges of developing an ecological standard for coastal and estuarine waters, a standard is not currently available.</p>

<p>Until a suitable standard is developed and confirmed, water and sewerage companies should plan improvements to storm overflows discharging to coastal and estuarine waters based on the target of not more than an average of 10 spills per annum. This is equivalent to the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> rainfall target and mirrors the long-established surrogate for the environment quality standards to protect shellfisheries.</p>

<h4 id="public-health-target">3.2.3 Public health target</h4>

<p>The <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> set an objective to protect the health of water users through the public health target:</p>

<p>“Water companies must significantly reduce harmful pathogens from storm overflows discharging near designated bathing waters, by either: applying disinfection; or reducing the frequency of discharges to meet <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> spill standards by 2035.”</p>

<h5 id="ea-bathing-water-spill-standards">3.2.3.1 <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> bathing water spill standards</h5>

<p><abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> spill standards are different for inland and coastal bathing waters.</p>

<p>For designated inland (rivers, lakes, and estuaries) bathing waters, storm overflows discharging directly into, or within 5km upstream of the upper limit of, the inland bathing water reach must be designed to achieve no more than an average of one spill per bathing season.</p>

<p>For coastal waters, storm overflows discharging within 1km upstream (and in hydraulic continuity) of designated bathing sites, must be designed to achieve:</p>

<ul>
  <li>no more than 3 spills per bathing season on average for ‘good’, ‘sufficient’ or ‘poor’ status</li>
  <li>no more than 2 spills per bathing season on average for ‘excellent’ status</li>
</ul>

<p>‘Average’ for design purposes should be assessed over a minimum of 10 years.</p>

<p>Designated bathing waters in estuaries should be designed to the same standards as those for coastal bathing waters, with the exception that where there is evidence that the designated bathing water is near the upstream freshwater limit and low salinities are observed, then these waters should be given the same protection as rivers (one spill per bathing season).</p>

<p>Water and sewerage companies should design to meet the coastal standards unless advised otherwise by the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>.</p>

<p>Further investigation by the water company will be required when a specific receiving water is not meeting bathing water standards despite nearby storm overflows meeting individual spill standards. For example, no more than 2 spills per bathing season on average for an ‘excellent’ bathing water.</p>

<p>In addition to the criteria above, the following apply:</p>

<ul>
  <li>if there is substantive evidence that concludes that bathing water quality is limited by the discharges from storm overflows that are located further away from the designated bathing water site than the distances set out above, the relevant investigation triggers listed above apply</li>
  <li>when the relevant <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> spill targets for human health are achieved, disinfection of discharges can be used to enhance water quality to meet bathing water standards – this is a clarification of the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr>’s targets</li>
</ul>

<p>Section 7 of this document sets out  spill standards in relation to soffit level (the level corresponding to the top of the outfall pipe).</p>

<h5 id="requirement-for-additional-works">3.2.3.2 Requirement for additional works</h5>

<p>Following completion of the spill reduction works, it may be found that the receiving water is not achieving its target public health quality as a result of storm overflow discharges.</p>

<p>In this situation, the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> should consider requiring the water and sewerage company to undertake an investigation and remedial scheme to secure no impacts on human health. In the first instance, this should be based on applying marine impact modelling to meet the following environmental quality standards (<abbr title="environmental quality standards">EQS</abbr>).</p>

<p><strong>Table: <abbr title="environmental quality standards">EQS</abbr> for faecal bacteria in coastal bathing waters</strong></p>

<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th scope="col">Bathing water class (2006 Bathing Water Directive)</th>
      <th scope="col">E. Coli standard (colony forming unit (CFU) per 100ml)</th>
      <th scope="col">Intestinal enterococci standard (CFU per 100ml)</th>
      <th scope="col">Standard type</th>
      <th scope="col">Maximum exceedance threshold (% of bathing season duration)</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>Sufficient</td>
      <td>500</td>
      <td>185</td>
      <td>90-percentile</td>
      <td>1.8</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Good</td>
      <td>500</td>
      <td>200</td>
      <td>95-percentile</td>
      <td>1.8</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Excellent</td>
      <td>250</td>
      <td>100</td>
      <td>95-percentile</td>
      <td>1.8</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<p>These standards apply to any location within the coastal water, not just the monitoring point. For standards for rivers and lakes, contact the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>.</p>

<p>Water and sewerage companies should not use these approaches to justify increasing spills above the default spills thresholds or existing levels.</p>

<h4 id="rainfall-target">3.2.4 Rainfall target</h4>

<p>The <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> rainfall target will ensure improvement of all storm overflows:</p>

<p>“Storm overflows will not be permitted to discharge above an average of 10 rainfall events per year by 2050.”</p>

<p>The maximum average 10 rainfall events target translates to water and sewerage companies designing, operating and maintaining their storm overflows and associated sewerage systems to ensure there are no more than 10 spills per year on average over a 10-year period. This is not limited to spills caused by rainfall.</p>

<p>The <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> rainfall target should not be interpreted as allowing an increase in spills up to 10 spills on average per year, such as due to the deterioration of asset performance.</p>

<h2 id="assessing-storm-overflows">4. Assessing storm overflows</h2>

<p>As set out in Section 2, water and sewerage companies must return event duration monitoring data annually to the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> for every storm overflow operated by a sewerage undertaker whose area is wholly or mainly in England. The data must contain the frequency and duration of all storm overflow spills.</p>

<p>This is a key step in water and sewerage companies and regulators being able to identify:</p>

<ul>
  <li>which storm overflows should be investigated</li>
  <li>where subsequent improvements are required</li>
</ul>

<p>This section provides an overarching approach to storm overflow investigations as agreed with the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> and Ofwat. Where needed, this may be complemented by further guidance from the regulators outlining technical detail on investigations.</p>

<p>It is ultimately the responsibility of water and sewerage companies to understand the obligations they need to meet and deliver action to achieve these. There may be circumstances in which ensuring compliance requires water and sewerage companies to go further than guidance set out by government or regulators.</p>

<h3 id="investigation-triggers">4.1 Investigation triggers</h3>

<p>A number of requirements need to be considered by water and sewerage companies when evaluating their assets. Assets can include storm overflows on the network or at wastewater treatment works.</p>

<p>Investigations are a common mechanism through which water and sewerage companies and regulators can:</p>

<ul>
  <li>evaluate an asset</li>
  <li>consider which requirements might apply</li>
  <li>determine whether action is required to deliver improvements</li>
</ul>

<p>There are currently around 14,500 storm overflows in England. Given the number of assets, it is reasonable for regulators to establish triggers for investigations in order to:</p>

<ul>
  <li>ensure that resources are used efficiently</li>
  <li>assist water and sewerage companies with prioritising the work which needs to be completed to achieve compliance with requirements in the most effective manner</li>
</ul>

<p>In the <abbr title="storm overflow assessment framework">SOAF</abbr> version 2, the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> sets triggers based on the frequency of spills to prioritise investigations in respect of the highest spilling storm overflows.</p>

<p>Through its enforcement proceedings, Ofwat has suggested a series of performance indicators, including spill levels. These should act as triggers for water and sewerage companies to proactively consider whether there may be compliance issues now or in the foreseeable future. Such consideration is part of water and sewerage companies’ obligations to ensure their assets are performing sufficiently.</p>

<p>The <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> and Ofwat investigation triggers align to form a complementary regulatory framework. If a storm overflow met or exceeded an investigation trigger set by the regulators, the water and sewerage company would be responsible for navigating the investigation process in section 4.2 and the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>’s <abbr title="storm overflow assessment framework">SOAF</abbr> version 2.</p>

<p>It is important to note that there is no single spill trigger set in law at which an investigation is required. While investigations can be triggered by meeting or exceeding a threshold, this is not the only route for identifying the need for improvements to be made to a storm overflow.</p>

<p>Water and sewerage companies have a responsibility to investigate a storm overflow discharging outside of ‘exceptional circumstances’, regardless of whether the asset has exceeded a spill trigger, as set out in Section 3.1.</p>

<p>Regulators may also decide to investigate water and sewerage companies and take enforcement action in circumstances other than those described in this document. For example, a storm overflow may not meet an investigation trigger, but if a permit condition were breached then the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> could investigate and take enforcement action in line with the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>’s enforcement and sanctions policy.</p>

<p>In addition to these investigation triggers, water and sewerage company <abbr title="drainage and wastewater management plans">DWMPs</abbr> contain spill ‘risk thresholds’ for strategic planning purposes. <abbr title="drainage and wastewater management plan">DWMP</abbr> risk thresholds use observed and modelled spills to forecast storm overflow performance, and investment needed, into the future.</p>

<p>The investigation triggers described in this document, Ofwat’s enforcement cases and the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>’s <abbr title="storm overflow assessment framework">SOAF</abbr> version 2 alert water and sewerage companies to more immediate issues with individual assets. These should be addressed to bring assets into compliance or prevent at risk assets becoming unsatisfactory or non-compliant, while <abbr title="drainage and wastewater management plan">DWMP</abbr> risk thresholds allow them to strategically plan investment and build resilience into their networks.</p>

<h3 id="investigation-process">4.2 Investigation process</h3>

<p>The investigation process involves gathering information and using this to understand the factors that have contributed to a storm overflow discharging and the impacts that the discharges are having.</p>

<p>To determine whether improvements may be required, water and sewerage companies should consider on a case-by-case basis:</p>

<ul>
  <li>all relevant legal requirements</li>
  <li>targets in the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr>
</li>
  <li>any other non-legislative requirements for their assets</li>
</ul>

<p>Water and sewerage companies should also consider whether there are deadlines by which these requirements must be met.</p>

<p>Through Ofwat’s price review business plan cycle, water and sewerage companies allocate funds for investigations against their statutory and non-statutory requirements. They will then schedule these during the asset management plan (<abbr title="asset management plan">AMP</abbr>) period in the most efficient way.</p>

<p>Where requirements for investigations emerge outside of the price review business planning process, such as mid-<abbr title="asset management plan">AMP</abbr>, water and sewerage companies should aim to carry these out as soon as feasibly possible. Where relevant, priority must be given to scheduling investigations which are linked to statutory requirements. For <abbr title="2024 price review">PR24</abbr>, further information is provided in Ofwat’s final determination documentation, which explains the storm overflows uncertainty mechanism they have put in place.</p>

<p>Investigations should be reviewed by companies periodically. Section 3.1.5 provides more information on the factors that may highlight the need to review a <abbr title="best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs">BTKNEEC</abbr> test or an investigation.</p>

<p>The <abbr title="storm overflow assessment framework">SOAF</abbr> version 2 outlines in detail the investigation process to be followed for storm overflows under the <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994 for both <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> and Ofwat investigation triggers.</p>

<h3 id="identifying-improvements">4.3 Identifying improvements</h3>

<p>As part of the investigation process, water and sewerage companies should develop and assess their options for improving a storm overflow, taking a number of different factors into consideration, as set out in this section and in the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>’s <abbr title="storm overflow assessment framework">SOAF</abbr> version 2.</p>

<p>If an appropriate improvement is identified, the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> will include improvement conditions in the permit to meet appropriate standards as soon as practicable. In some circumstances, the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> may identify a storm overflow as impacting the environment or human health outside of the usual investigation process proactively require improvements through permit variation.</p>

<p>The process of identifying potential improvements is not limited to the 5-yearly price review cycle. At times, water and sewerage companies will be required to develop and assess their options for improving storm overflows more frequently, to comply with their legal obligations.</p>

<h4 id="optioneering">4.3.1 Optioneering</h4>

<p>Water and sewerage companies should be able to demonstrate to regulators that they have considered a range of options when identifying and designing their schemes to improve storm overflows. This could include:</p>

<ul>
  <li>grey infrastructure</li>
  <li>green infrastructure</li>
  <li>grey and green hybrid improvements</li>
  <li>improvements to reduce demands on sewerage assets</li>
  <li>improvements that increase capacity</li>
  <li>innovative alternative improvements</li>
</ul>

<p>Water and sewerage companies should consider not only the capital and operational (Totex) costs of improvements, but also the carbon (embedded and operational) and additional societal and nature-based benefits of each option.</p>

<p>It is important that standards, assessments and upgrades focus on the site or specific overflow under consideration. However, when deciding on options, water and sewerage companies should consider a catchment approach alongside an asset-by-asset approach where appropriate. This is not a new expectation: companies should already be applying a catchment approach in other areas of planning, such as in <abbr title="drainage and wastewater management plans">DWMPs</abbr>.</p>

<p>For example, by considering the benefits that storm overflow improvements may offer on a wider level than just the individual asset, particularly where there are significant environmental issues which cannot be improved in a cost beneficial way simply by remediating one asset.</p>

<p>When deciding on and comparing options, water and sewerage companies should also consider the different timeframes for delivery, particularly if there is a regulatory deadline.</p>

<h4 id="optioneering-based-on-wastewater-supply-and-demand-modelling">4.3.2 Optioneering based on wastewater supply and demand modelling</h4>

<p>Water and sewerage company optioneering of storm overflow improvements should consider demand- as well as supply-based options within the context of wastewater supply demand (also known as wastewater flow or capacity). </p>

<p>Supply-based options, such as increasing capacity of the sewerage network or increased treatment capacity, usually rely upon grey infrastructure, or in some cases a hybrid grey and green infrastructure, such as constructed wetlands. </p>

<p>Demand-based options, including surface water diversion away from combined sewers or its attenuation, are considered more sustainable as they relieve pressure on sewerage systems now and in the future, whereas supply-based options often require upgrading as pressures increase in the future. Demand-based options also reduce the ongoing costs of treatment and conveyance (such as pumping), so have smaller revenue costs and smaller operational carbon over their lifetime.</p>

<h4 id="green-infrastructure">4.3.3 Green infrastructure</h4>

<p>The <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> promotes and encourages low carbon and green improvements to addressing storm overflow spills.</p>

<p>Green infrastructure and other nature-based improvements can be an effective option to reduce the harm caused by storm overflows and can provide multiple co-benefits for the environment and society. For example, separating surface water so that it does not mix with sewage and is diverted to water gardens or wetlands:</p>

<ul>
  <li>improves water quality</li>
  <li>creates new habitats for species</li>
  <li>acts as a carbon sink</li>
</ul>

<p><abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> expects the adoption of green infrastructure, either wholly or partly, to be encouraged by the regulators in line with their own legal duties and where it can meet water and sewerage companies’ legal requirements.</p>

<p>The regulators retain some flexibility when working with water and sewerage companies on the timeframes for delivering green infrastructure improvements (see section 5.2). Water and sewerage companies can further discuss the delivery of green infrastructure improvements with the regulators as needed, on a site or catchment basis.</p>

<p>Water and sewerage companies should investigate and introduce green infrastructure at the upstream end of catchments. This is linked to the expectation that water and sewerage companies will consider a catchment approach when optioneering, where appropriate (see section 4.3.1). Upstream improvements often provide greater societal benefits and have lower carbon cost compared to green infrastructure implemented in the downstream area of a catchment.</p>

<p>The environmental benefits of green infrastructure projects may take some time to be realised, and so may not be achieved before the target dates specified in the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr>. As such, these projects can still be counted towards achieving the targets if they are started before 2027 and delivered as quickly as possible. Promoting the use of green infrastructure to achieve the targets in the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> will continue to be subject to review.</p>

<p>Green infrastructure improvements to storm overflows can be both supply- and demand-based. These improvements have advantages in that they can in some cases lead to lower embedded carbon and have lower operational carbon emissions than typical grey infrastructure improvements.</p>

<p>On the commencement of section 5 of the Water (Special Measures) Act 2025, water and sewerage companies’ statutory <abbr title="drainage and wastewater management plans">DWMPs</abbr> will have to detail the use that is to be made of nature-based solutions, technologies and facilities within the undertaker’s drainage system and sewerage system.</p>

<h2 id="delivering-storm-overflow-improvements">5. Delivering storm overflow improvements</h2>

<p>Once a storm overflow has been assessed under <abbr title="storm overflow assessment framework">SOAF</abbr> version 2, and if it has been determined that there is an appropriate solution for improvement, water and sewerage companies must plan and deliver these improvements so that they comply with relevant legal and policy requirements.</p>

<p><abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> and the regulators understand the need to take into account the deliverability, affordability and financeability of investment required to improve storm overflow performance over time. While meeting regulatory requirements, including fixed regulatory deadlines, must be a water company’s priority, consideration should be given by regulators where appropriate to the timing of improvements being phased over multiple asset management periods.</p>

<p>This will support delivery, ensure affordability to customers, and ensure water and sewerage companies can attract the necessary investment in alignment with <abbr title="asset management plan">AMP</abbr> cycles. For the <abbr title="2024 price review">PR24</abbr> period, further detail is provided in Ofwat’s final determination documents.</p>

<p>This section suggests considerations for regulators and water and sewerage companies to help ensure improvement plans are affordable, financeable and deliverable.</p>

<h3 id="improving-storm-overflows-under-the-uwwtr-1994-and-the-sodrp">5.1 Improving storm overflows under the <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994 and the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr>
</h3>

<p>The <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994 and the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> share the same overall ambition: to reduce the harm caused by storm overflow discharges. Despite a shared ambition, the action that water and sewerage companies would need to take to meet <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994 requirements may sometimes differ from what is needed to meet <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> targets.</p>

<p>In order to identify which of the drivers requires the most environmentally beneficial results, a storm overflow improvement required under <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994 (having satisfied the <abbr title="best technical knowledge not entailing excessive costs">BTKNEEC</abbr> test) should be considered alongside other improvements to meet legal requirements and action to meet the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> targets.</p>

<p>For example, an assessment under the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>’s <abbr title="storm overflow assessment framework">SOAF</abbr> version 2 could find that in order to satisfy <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994 requirements, a particular storm overflow should be improved so that it spills no more than 13 times per year.</p>

<p>If that same storm overflow was discharging into or near a site of special scientific interest (<abbr title="site of special scientific interest">SSSI</abbr>), this would be classed as a ‘high priority site’ under the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr>. Under the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> the storm overflow would need to be improved to meet both the ecological target, and the rainfall target.</p>

<p>This might result in the storm overflow needing to be improved so that it spills fewer than 10 times on average per year, or a lower spill frequency to eliminate ecological harm. Its ‘high priority site’ status would also influence the timing of the improvement.</p>

<p>In this case, the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> requirements would be more stringent than the <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> requirements. Taking action in line with the most stringent requirements would result in greater benefits for the environment and public health.</p>

<p>Where possible, <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> recommends that water and sewerage companies design improvement options which fulfil all the relevant requirements for the storm overflow being assessed, minimising situations where multiple improvements are made to the same asset.</p>

<p>There may be circumstances in which this approach is not feasible or would result in unacceptable delays to compliance with the legislation, and so a more modular approach may therefore be more appropriate.</p>

<p>In all circumstances, water and sewerage companies must fulfil their legal obligations on storm overflows, and as such prioritise the delivery of storm overflow improvements which are required in law.</p>

<p>Ultimately, it is for water and sewerage companies to determine the most effective way of complying with their legal requirements and meeting the targets set out in the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr>. The interplay between <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> and <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994 requirements should not be used as a reason to delay improvements.</p>

<h3 id="timeframes-for-delivery">5.2 Timeframes for delivery</h3>

<p>Government expects water and sewerage companies to achieve compliance by delivering improvements as fast as possible, with regulators incentivising and monitoring this delivery.</p>

<p>Given the challenges associated with the scale and complexity of investment on storm overflows, with some improvements needing to be delivered over several price review periods, it is important that the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> and Ofwat retain some flexibility when working with water and sewerage companies on the timeframe for improvements.</p>

<p>When regulators engage with water and sewerage companies on the planning and sequencing of storm overflow improvements, they should give consideration to the following factors:</p>

<ul>
  <li>prioritisation of storm overflow improvements (for example, meeting legal requirements or target achievement dates)</li>
  <li>environmental and public health outcomes</li>
  <li>deliverability, affordability and financeability of improvements at a project and programme level</li>
</ul>

<p>When fulfilling their statutory duties on storm overflows, regulators will take all appropriate factors into consideration.</p>

<h3 id="distinguishing-between-maintenance-improvements-and-longer-term-improvements">5.3 Distinguishing between maintenance improvements and longer-term improvements</h3>

<p>In many cases, compliance issues can be addressed through basic operational changes, repairs and maintenance. These types of improvements have been provided for and continue to be provided for through water and sewerage companies’ base revenue allowances and should be reflected in statutory <abbr title="drainage and wastewater management plans">DWMPs</abbr> on an ongoing basis.</p>

<p>Water and sewerage companies should not delay the implementation of such improvements in favour of a longer-term build solution, or by waiting for annual <abbr title="event duration monitor">EDM</abbr> returns where a problem has been identified.</p>

<h3 id="the-role-of-government-and-regulators-in-overseeing-planning-and-delivery-of-improvements">5.4 The role of government and regulators in overseeing planning and delivery of improvements</h3>

<p>Government and regulators have responsibilities in relation to the planning and delivery of improvements and work together to support each other in delivery of their respective remits, consistent with their statutory duties. However, they have different areas of primary focus, reflective of their areas of expertise.</p>

<h4 id="the-environment-agencys-role-in-planning-and-overseeing-delivery-of-improvements">5.4.1 The Environment Agency’s role in planning and overseeing delivery of improvements </h4>

<p>The <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> takes the lead in identifying the obligations for water and sewerage companies in the water industry strategic environmental requirements (<abbr title="water industry strategic environmental requirements">WISER</abbr>) guidance.</p>

<p>The <abbr title="water industry strategic environmental requirements">WISER</abbr> guidance covers the issues and opportunities water and sewerage companies should consider when meeting their environmental obligations, including, but not limited to, improvements on storm overflows.</p>

<p>Obligations identified in the <abbr title="water industry strategic environmental requirements">WISER</abbr> guidance for storm overflows then translate into measures and actions identified through the water industry national environment programme (<abbr title="water industry national environment programme">WINEP</abbr>).</p>

<p>The <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> works with water and sewerage companies to identify suitable schemes to meet these obligations and reviews draft <abbr title="water industry national environment programme">WINEP</abbr> measures ahead of final determination of price review allowances by Ofwat.</p>

<p>The <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> also:</p>

<ul>
  <li>assesses the progress of these storm overflow improvements by tracking delivery of the <abbr title="water industry national environment programme">WINEP</abbr> measures, and where changes are made, effecting these changes in the applicable permits</li>
  <li>oversees the delivery of the most cost-beneficial solution as identified through the <abbr title="storm overflow assessment framework">SOAF</abbr> in order to reduce environmental impact, frequency of discharges or both, subject to appropriate prioritisation</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="ofwats-role-in-planning-and-overseeing-delivery-of-improvements">5.4.2 Ofwat’s role in planning and overseeing delivery of improvements</h4>

<p>Ofwat takes the lead in setting revenue allowances through their price review for the efficient investment companies need to fulfil their legal obligations and service commitments to customers, including in relation to storm overflows.</p>

<p>This price review process is informed by business plans put forward by water and sewerage companies. These plans are then reviewed by Ofwat as part of their final determination process.</p>

<p>Ofwat continues to take into account the affordability, financeability and deliverability of these plans, working with the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> and government as necessary to ensure water and sewerage companies have clarity on their long-term investment requirements and funding landscape.</p>

<p>Ofwat also incentivises water and sewerage companies to deliver against their commitments, through:</p>

<ul>
  <li>performance commitments</li>
  <li>price control deliverables</li>
  <li>returning money to customers if these are not delivered</li>
</ul>

<p><a rel="external" href="https://www.ofwat.gov.uk/regulated-companies/price-review/2024-price-review/framework-and-methodology/final-methodology/pr24-performance-commitment-definitions/"><abbr title="2024 price review">PR24</abbr> includes performance commitments (ofwat.gov.uk)</a>, with financial consequences based on the average number of storm overflow spills, to encourage water and sewerage companies to address high spilling sites. Through this process, Ofwat will identify:</p>

<ul>
  <li>works which are funded through base spend, such as operational and maintenance</li>
  <li>spill reduction improvements which are funded through enhancement expenditure</li>
</ul>

<p>The <a rel="external" href="https://www.ofwat.gov.uk/publication/storm-overflows-pc-definition/">storm overflows performance commitments definition (ofwat.gov.uk)</a>  was published in June 2023.</p>

<h4 id="defras-role-in-planning-and-overseeing-and-delivery-of-improvements">5.4.3 <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr>’s role in planning and overseeing and delivery of improvements</h4>

<p>Among other things, <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> has responsibility for setting the overall direction of storm overflows policy, including targets and legislation.</p>

<p>This includes issuing strategic policy statements to Ofwat, outlining <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr>’s priorities for the regulation of the water industry ahead of price reviews.</p>

<p>Through this process, <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> seeks to ensure clarity and predictability for the sector, consulting on any significant changes at the earliest stage, to ensure water and sewerage companies have the stability they need for their long-term planning and to secure a pipeline of investment for the required improvements.</p>

<p><abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> also signs off the water industry strategic environmental requirements (<abbr title="water industry strategic environmental requirements">WISER</abbr>).</p>

<h2 id="enforcement">6. Enforcement</h2>

<p>Where there are legal requirements in relation to storm overflows or the discharges from them, it is the responsibility of water and sewerage companies to:</p>

<ul>
  <li>understand those requirements</li>
  <li>assess whether the design and operation of their assets comply with the requirements</li>
  <li>take necessary action in an appropriate timeframe to ensure that they are, and remain, in compliance with those requirements</li>
</ul>

<p>If there are concerns about non-compliance, it is for the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> and Ofwat to take appropriate steps to investigate further and take enforcement action where appropriate.</p>

<h3 id="the-environment-agencys-role-in-storm-overflow-enforcement">6.1 The Environment Agency’s role in storm overflow enforcement </h3>

<p>The <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>’s role in relation to enforcement includes:</p>

<ul>
  <li>exercising their duty under regulation 6 of the <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994 to carry out their functions under the <abbr title="Environmental Permitting (England and Wales) Regulations 2016">EPR 2016</abbr> to secure limitation of pollution of receiving waters due to storm water overflows – this duty is applicable when the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> is exercising their enforcement functions</li>
  <li>taking enforcement action where they are satisfied that a permit condition has been breached, in accordance with their enforcement and sanctions policy – enforcement action may result in enforcement notices, civil sanctions or criminal prosecutions</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="ofwats-role-in-storm-overflow-enforcement">6.2 Ofwat’s role in storm overflow enforcement</h3>

<p>Ofwat’s role in relation to enforcement includes fulfilling their duty under section 18 of the <abbr title="Water Industry Act 1991">WIA 1991</abbr> to impose an enforcement order on a company where they are satisfied that there is, or is likely to be, a breach of either:</p>

<ul>
  <li>section 94 of the <abbr title="Water Industry Act 1991">WIA 1991</abbr>
</li>
