  <li>regulation 4 of the <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994</li>
</ul>

<p>Such an enforcement order is to secure the company’s compliance.</p>

<p>Section 19 of the <abbr title="Water Industry Act 1991">WIA 1991</abbr> provides exceptions to Ofwat’s duty under section 18, where the breach is of a trivial nature. It also provides an exception where either:</p>

<ul>
  <li>the company has given and is complying with an undertaking to secure its compliance</li>
  <li>an enforcement order would be inconsistent with Ofwat’s duties under Chapter 2 of Part 1 <abbr title="Water Industry Act 1991">WIA 1991</abbr>
</li>
</ul>

<p>If a company fails to comply with such an undertaking, Ofwat has a duty under section 18 of the <abbr title="Water Industry Act 1991">WIA 1991</abbr> to impose an enforcement order to secure compliance.</p>

<p>Section 22A of the <abbr title="Water Industry Act 1991">WIA 1991</abbr> allows Ofwat to impose financial penalties, where they are satisfied that a company has breached or is breaching a relevant legal obligation. Ofwat will consider a number of factors in determining the appropriate level of such a penalty in the circumstances of each breach. Financial penalties imposed in accordance with this provision cannot exceed 10% of a company’s relevant turnover in the preceding business year.</p>

<p>On a case-by-case basis, and where their powers allow them to do so, Ofwat will consider regulatory settlement. Where accepted, this would require an undertaking to be agreed, setting out:</p>

<ul>
  <li>the remedial steps Ofwat considers appropriate to secure compliance</li>
  <li>appropriate financial and non-financial commitments, such as a redress package for customers or remediation of harm caused by the identified breach</li>
</ul>

<p>Such regulatory settlement may be accepted in lieu of all or part of a proposed financial penalty.</p>

<p>Before making an enforcement order or imposing a financial penalty, Ofwat is required to consider whether it would be more appropriate to proceed using their powers under the Competition Act 1998.</p>

<h3 id="defras-role-in-storm-overflow-enforcement">6.3 <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr>’s role in storm overflow enforcement</h3>

<p><abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr>’s role includes:</p>

<ul>
  <li>responsibility for setting the overall direction of storm overflows policy, including targets and legislation</li>
  <li>general strategic oversight of the storm overflows regulatory system</li>
  <li>establishing the strategic policy direction and the overarching legislative framework within which regulators operate and ensuring these remain up to date with the best available information on environmental needs and the water industry</li>
</ul>

<p>This includes issuing strategic policy statements to Ofwat outlining <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr>’s priorities for the regulation of the water industry ahead of price reviews. Ofwat has a legal duty to carry out their functions in accordance with a strategic policy statement, as set out in section 2A of the <abbr title="Water Industry Act 1991">WIA 1991</abbr>.</p>

<p><abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> also meets regularly with the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> and Ofwat to retain an understanding of:</p>

<ul>
  <li>water and sewerage company performance</li>
  <li>how the regulators are exercising their enforcement duties more generally</li>
</ul>

<p>This is while ensuring that the regulators retain required independence on individual cases and enforcement proceedings.</p>

<p><abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> recognises the jurisdiction of the regulators in enforcing compliance with relevant statutory or non-statutory requirements.</p>

<p>As an example, <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> expects the regulators to utilise data on storm overflows obtained via <abbr title="event duration monitors">EDMs</abbr> (and other relevant monitoring programmes as they become available) to inform their assessment of water company performance and compliance. However, it is for the regulators to decide:</p>

<ul>
  <li>which other sources of information are necessary in order to form a view on these matters</li>
  <li>how any investigation processes should be carried out</li>
  <li>ultimately what the outcome of these investigations are</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="replacing-sections-of-the-1997-guidance">7. Replacing sections of the 1997 guidance</h2>

<p>Draft guidance on the <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994 was issued to dischargers and regulators in July 1997 (the 1997 guidance). It was intended as a working document on the implementation and interpretation of the <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994.</p>

<p>Except for a limited update in 2009, the 1997 guidance has not been revised since it was published. As discussed throughout this document, there have been considerable changes in the storm overflows policy landscape in recent years, including the issuance of the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> and increased awareness and evidence due to 100% storm overflow <abbr title="event duration monitor">EDM</abbr> coverage. In addition, technical knowledge relating to water quality has progressed.</p>

<p>Within the 1997 guidance, information related to storm overflows is largely contained within Annex 8, entitled ‘Framework for Consenting Intermittent Discharges’. Annex 3, entitled ‘Design, Construction and Operation of Collecting Systems and Treatment Plant’, also refers to the operation of storm overflows (as part of the wider sewerage system).</p>

<p>All of Annex 8 to the 1997 guidance, to the extent that it had not already been superseded, is now withdrawn in respect of storm overflows operated by water and sewerage companies whose areas are wholly or mainly in England, and superseded by this publication in 2025. This does not apply to storm overflows operated by water and sewerage companies whose areas are wholly or mainly in Wales.</p>

<p>We have also provided updated references for the design, construction and operation of collecting systems, in place of the references found in Annex 3 of the 1997 guidance.</p>

<p>The rest of the 1997 guidance is not being withdrawn at this stage but may be updated in future.</p>

<p>The following sections have been provided by the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>, as the technical expert on storm overflows regulation. Further updates to the sections below may be provided by the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> as appropriate.</p>

<h3 id="helpful-references-for-the-design-construction-and-operation-of-collecting-systems">7.1 Helpful references for the design, construction and operation of collecting systems</h3>

<p>The principal document that defines current practice for the design, construction and operation of collecting systems is BS EN 752:2017 “Drain and sewer systems outside buildings – sewer system management”. Other relevant supporting documentation includes:</p>

<ul>
  <li><a rel="external" href="https://fwr.org/publication/urban-pollution-manual-upm/">Urban Pollution Management 3rd Edition (2018)</a></li>
  <li><a rel="external" href="https://www.ciwem.org/assets/uploads/CIWEM_UDG_EDM_Good_Practice_Guide_2021_final.pdf"><abbr title="Chartered Institution of Water and Environmental Management">CIWEM</abbr> Event Duration Monitoring Good Practice Guide</a></li>
  <li><a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/review-of-urban-pollution-management-standards-against-water-framework-directive-requirements">review of urban pollution management standards against <abbr title="Water Framework Directive">WFD</abbr> requirements</a></li>
  <li><a rel="external" href="https://www.ciwem.org/special-interest-groups/urban-drainage-group">guidance notes and codes of practice published by the <abbr title="Chartered Institution of Water and Environmental Management">CIWEM</abbr> Urban Drainage Group</a></li>
  <li>drainage and wastewater management plan guidelines</li>
</ul>

<p>A number of documents deal with storm overflows and use of rainfall time series for sewer system modelling. These include the following:</p>

<ul>
  <li><a rel="external" href="https://www.ciwem.org/assets/pdf/Special%20Interest%20Groups/Urban%20Drainage%20Group/CIWEM-UDG-Rainfall-Guide-2016.pdf"><abbr title="Chartered Institution of Water and Environmental Management">CIWEM</abbr> Rainfall Modelling Guide</a></li>
  <li><a rel="external" href="https://www.ciwem.org/assets/pdf/Special%20Interest%20Groups/Urban%20Drainage%20Group/Code%20of%20Practice%20for%20the%20Hydraulic%20Modelling%20of%20Ur.pdf"><abbr title="Chartered Institution of Water and Environmental Management">CIWEM</abbr> Code of Practice for the Hydraulic Modelling of Urban Drainage Systems</a></li>
  <li><a rel="external" href="https://ukwir.org/eng/reports/15-CL-10-16-1/129641/Rainfall-Intensity-for-Sewer-Design--Technical-Guide">UK Water Industry Research (<abbr title="UK Water Industry Research">UKWIR</abbr>) Rainfall Intensity for Sewer Design - Technical Guide</a></li>
  <li><a rel="external" href="https://ukwir.org/eng/climate-change-rainfall-for-use-in-sewerage-design-design-storm-profiles-antecedent-conditions-redup-tool-update-and-seasonality-impacts-guidance"><abbr title="UK Water Industry Research">UKWIR</abbr> Climate Change Rainfall for use in Sewerage Design – Design Storm Profiles, Antecedent Conditions, RED-UP Tool Update and Seasonality Impacts Guidance</a></li>
</ul>

<p>The <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> uses the <a rel="external" href="https://ukwir.org/ukwir-redup-tool"><abbr title="UK Water Industry Research">UKWIR</abbr> RED-UP</a> tool for creating climate perturbed rainfall time series in the <abbr title="storm overflow assessment framework">SOAF</abbr> version 2, and <a rel="external" href="https://www.ceh.ac.uk/our-science/projects/eflag-enhanced-future-flows-and-groundwater">eFLaG</a> for guidance on flow. Separate guidance will be available for surface water temperature uplifts once published.</p>

<p>Reference should be made to the <abbr title="Chartered Institution of Water and Environmental Management">CIWEM</abbr> Urban Drainage Group guidance ‘<a rel="external" href="https://www.ciwem.org/assets/pdf/Special%20Interest%20Groups/Urban%20Drainage%20Group/The-Design-of-CSO-Chambers-to-Incorporate-Screens.pdf"><abbr title="Wastewater Planning Users Group">WaPUG</abbr> Guide: The Design of <abbr title="combined sewer overflow">CSO</abbr> Chambers to Incorporate Screens’</a> and any future updates of this.</p>

<h3 id="framework-for-permitting-storm-overflows">7.2 Framework for permitting storm overflows</h3>

<h4 id="introduction-1">7.2.1 Introduction</h4>

<p>This section sets out criteria for the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>’s permitting of those overflows that are unsatisfactory. This is not a complete methodology for determining permit or <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> compliance. It is intended as a guideline to provide clarity for water and sewerage companies. Companies should also refer to the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>’s latest guidance and relevant legal requirements.</p>

<p>Unsettled storm overflows at sewage treatment works will be considered in the same manner as network storm overflows under the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr>. Clearly, if one is unsatisfactory according to the criteria below, it should be treated in the same way as any other storm overflow, but this may need to be tied in with a review of the permit for the whole works.</p>

<h4 id="definition-of-unsatisfactory-and-at-risk-storm-overflows">7.2.2 Definition of ‘unsatisfactory’ and ‘at risk’ storm overflows</h4>

<p>The following table is to be used by the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> in deciding which storm overflows are unsatisfactory and, therefore, subject to permit review to drive improvements.</p>

<p>The criteria given in the table below are largely objective, although some subjectivity may apply. In particular, some discretion must be left for local interpretation of the significance and contribution of an overflow to a particular problem.</p>

<p>Criteria to identify ‘at risk storm overflows’ are set out in the table in this section. These overflows are not yet unsatisfactory but are at risk of becoming unsatisfactory if action is not taken as they currently cross accepted performance thresholds, however the timeframe to improve them to meet these thresholds set out in plans has not yet been exceeded.</p>

<p>Examples of situations where a storm overflow could be considered ‘at risk’ of becoming unsatisfactory include where:</p>

<ul>
  <li>it does not meet set standards of engineering and aesthetic control for storm overflows (for example, no screen yet installed) but not yet passed the date specified in the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> for all storm overflows to be screened</li>
  <li>current spill performance exceeds thresholds set in the <abbr title="storm overflow assessment framework">SOAF</abbr>, but the investigation (which is being progressed) has not yet concluded that spill reduction is required</li>
  <li>current spill performance exceeds thresholds set in the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr>, but not yet passed the date specified in the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> for all storm overflows to meet these thresholds</li>
  <li>there is confirmed local adverse ecological impact, but not yet passed the relevant date in the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> for the storm overflow to meet these thresholds</li>
  <li>it does not have sufficient hydraulic capacity compared to accepted minimum design standards</li>
</ul>

<p>Issues identified through an investigation into an at risk overflow that could result in the storm overflow becoming unsatisfactory should be addressed proactively. Issues identified that are not sufficient to risk the storm overflow becoming unsatisfactory should be reflected in and addressed as part of subsequent integrated programmes of work within the catchments, including <abbr title="drainage and wastewater management plans">DWMPs</abbr>.</p>

<p>If an overflow becomes unsatisfactory, the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> can review the water and sewerage company’s permit or take enforcement action if there is a breach of the existing permit.</p>

<p>The <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> can include an improvement condition in permits for unsatisfactory storm overflows to meet the appropriate standards as soon as practicable.</p>

<p><abbr title="water industry national environment programme">WINEP</abbr> investigations and improvements should be aligned to achieve the targets set out in the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> through the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>’s <abbr title="water industry national environment programme">WINEP</abbr> guidance prior to each <abbr title="asset management plan">AMP</abbr> cycle.</p>

</td>
      <td>Discharges above an average of 10 spill events per year.</td>
      <td>Annual <abbr title="event duration monitor">EDM</abbr> data shows spills in excess of target spills per annum, following guidance from the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Shellfish</th>
      <td>Discharges near designated shellfisheries: <br><br>After 2030: causes or significantly contribute to failures in shellfish quality standards for identified shellfish waters.<br><br>After 2050: frequency of discharge exceeds 10 spills per year</td>
      <td>Annual <abbr title="event duration monitor">EDM</abbr> data shows spills in excess of target spills per annum, following guidance from the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>.<br><br>‘near’ – overflows discharging within 1km hydraulic continuity of designated shellfish waters</td>
      <td>For discharges near designated shellfisheries, the following criteria apply:<br><br> 1. The storm overflow causes or significantly contribute to failures in shellfish quality standards for identified shellfish waters.<br>2. The frequency of discharge exceeds 10 spills per year.</td>
      <td>Annual <abbr title="event duration monitor">EDM</abbr> data shows spills in excess of target spills per annum, following guidance from the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>. <br><br>‘near’ – overflows discharging within 1km hydraulic continuity of designated shellfish waters.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Groundwater impact</th>
      <td>Cause pollution of groundwater</td>
      <td>Not applicable</td>
      <td>Not applicable</td>
      <td>Not applicable</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Asset standard</th>
      <td>None</td>
      <td>Not applicable</td>
      <td>Does not have sufficient hydraulic capacity compared to accepted minimum design standards</td>
      <td>Formula A <br><br>3PG+ I + 3E <br><br>Groundwater inundated sewerage system</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<h4 id="definitions-to-inform-the-permitting-of-storm-overflows">7.2.3 Definitions to inform the permitting of storm overflows</h4>

<p>The following definitions are relevant for storm overflows discharging into freshwater, coastal waters and estuaries.</p>

<h5 id="dry-weather-flow-dwf">Dry weather flow (<abbr title="dry weather flow">DWF</abbr>)</h5>

<p>For design purposes <abbr title="dry weather flow">DWF</abbr> is calculated by the equation ‘<abbr title="dry weather flow">DWF</abbr> = PG + I<sub>MAX</sub> + E’, where:</p>

<ul>
  <li>P = population served</li>
  <li>G = water consumption per head per day</li>
  <li>I<sub>MAX</sub> = maximum infiltration rate over the whole year</li>
  <li>E = trade effluent flow to sewer as applicable</li>
</ul>

<h5 id="formula-a">Formula A</h5>

<p>Formula A is a storm overflow setting as defined in the Report of the Technical Committee on Storm Overflows and the Disposal of Storm Sewage (1970).</p>

<p>The formula should be amended, as described in the report, for any separate areas within the sewer catchment. Where storage is provided at a storm overflow, and in very large sewerage systems where significant smoothing of flows occurs, this will be taken into account in defining the performance equivalent to ‘Formula A’ without storage.</p>

<p>The standard ‘Formula A’ is <abbr title="dry weather flow">DWF</abbr> + 1360P + 2E, where flows are expressed in litres per day, but minor local variations have been developed and are acceptable provided they are fully documented.</p>

<h5 id="soffit-level">Soffit level</h5>

<p>Soffit level is the level of the top inner surface of the outfall pipe.</p>

<h5 id="mean-low-water-of-spring-tides-mlws">Mean low water of spring tides (<abbr title="mean low water level of springtides">MLWS</abbr>)</h5>

<p><abbr title="mean low water level of springtides">MLWS</abbr> is the level of ‘mean low water spring tides’ as given in the Admiralty Tide Tables and corrected, where necessary, for the actual location of the outfall.</p>

<h5 id="estuarine-waters">Estuarine waters</h5>

<p>Estuarine waters are all waters defined as estuarine in regulation 2(1) of the <abbr title="Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations">UWWTR</abbr> 1994.</p>

<h5 id="coastal-waters">Coastal waters</h5>

<p>Coastal waters are all marine waters up to the 3 nautical mile limit, excluding estuaries.</p>

<h4 id="normal-requirements-for-storm-overflows">7.2.4 Normal requirements for storm overflows</h4>

<p>The following requirements will normally apply to water and sewerage companies with storm overflows which discharge into freshwaters. The <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> will assess whether companies are complying with these requirements. This list is non-exhaustive.</p>

<p>The sewerage system must be designed so that discharges are not made until the incoming flow exceeds that calculated from ‘Formula A’, as defined above.</p>

<p>The discharge should not create any visual or aesthetic impact caused by solids, paper, plastic or fungus as demonstrated by a history of justified public complaints or concern.</p>

<p>As set out in the <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr>, water and sewerage companies should install 6mm screens on every storm overflow when making improvements to meet <abbr title="storm overflows discharge reduction plan">SODRP</abbr> targets.</p>

<p>Screening controls are defined as 6mm solids separation: separation from the effluent, of a significant quantity of persistent material, and faecal and organic solids, greater than 6mm in any 2 dimensions. Screens should be designed to operate effectively up to the 1 in 5-year flow rate.</p>

<p>Screens should be installed into a chamber which meets the latest design guidance available.</p>

<p>The normal minimum design requirement is for all sewage flows up to 3PG + I<sub>MAX</sub> + 3E to be fully treated (flow to full treatment (<abbr title="flow to full treatment">FFT</abbr>)). Flow between <abbr title="flow to full treatment">FFT</abbr> (normally designed at 3PG + I<sub>MAX</sub> + 3E) and 6PG + I<sub>MAX</sub> + 3E or Formula A should normally have tank treatment provided by storm tank capacity of 68 l per hd or 2 hours at 3PG + I<sub>MAX</sub> + 3E as appropriate or by a process giving equivalent performance. Flows greater than 6PG + I<sub>MAX</sub> + 3E should be dealt with as storm overflows.</p>

<p>Permits issued must include necessary conditions such as overflow location, type, weir setting, storage requirements, and aesthetic performance standards. Permits may also contain spill frequency performance targets. The <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr> will not normally consider it necessary to apply chemical and bacteriological quality conditions in the permit unless the solution relies upon treatment.</p>

<h4 id="additional-requirements-for-storm-overflows-discharging-to-coastal-and-estuarine-waters">7.2.5 Additional requirements for storm overflows discharging to coastal and estuarine waters</h4>

<p>Further control of combined sewage overflows to coastal and estuarine tidal waters is needed to ensure that, where waters are identified under the provisions of the Bathing Water Directive, compliance with the requirements of that directive is not compromised by the adverse effect of such discharges.</p>

<p>It is recognised that there are distinct variations in the nature of receiving coastal and estuarine waters. This publication is therefore designed to take into account local conditions and provide a framework for issuing permits which reflect the local needs and benefits to the environment.</p>

<p>The need to limit the operation of tidal storm overflows and provide emission control of sewage solids through the use of appropriate solids retention techniques is also described.</p>

<p>In general, subject to specified exceptional circumstances, the following requirements will apply as a minimum:</p>

<p>Minimum retained flow: The sewerage system should be designed so that the storm overflow will not spill until the incoming flow exceeds that calculated from ‘Formula A’, or equivalent. The Formula is to be amended as described in the report of the Technical Committee on Storm Overflows and the Disposal of Storm Sewage (1970) for any separate areas within the sewered catchment.</p>

<p>The paragraphs in relation to the normal minimum design requirement and necessary permit conditions in section 7.2.4, also apply here.</p>

<p>Location: The outfall soffit level of all storm overflows must be located below the level of low water mark of mean spring tides (<abbr title="mean low water level of springtides">MLWS</abbr>).</p>

<p>Where there are particular local extenuating circumstances which either prevent or render it impractical to locate the outfall in accordance with the minimum requirement, then the following guidance should be applied, appropriate to the receiving water category.</p>

<p>A spill frequency standard should be applied as follows:</p>

<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th scope="col">Soffit level</th>
      <th scope="col">Operational setting</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>Storm overflow soffit above <abbr title="mean low water level of springtides">MLWS</abbr> but below the level of high water of mean spring tides (<abbr title="mean high water level of springtides">MHWS</abbr>)</td>
      <td>Spill frequency should be set between 3 spills per season and 1 spill in every 5 bathing seasons based on local considerations and the actual location of the storm overflow soffit.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Storm overflow soffit at <abbr title="mean high water level of springtides">MHWS</abbr>
</td>
      <td>Spill frequency should be limited to 1 spill in every 5 bathing seasons.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Storm overflow soffit above <abbr title="mean high water level of springtides">MHWS</abbr>
</td>
      <td>Spill frequency should be limited to 1 spill in every 5 years.</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<p>For short sea outfalls located within designated bathing waters, these sites will still impact bathing waters, but the operational settings will be determined with reference to the <abbr title="Environment Agency">EA</abbr>’s bathing water guidance (2018).</p>

<p>Where the water and sewerage company intends to extend the outfall of the storm overflow some distance offshore of <abbr title="mean low water level of springtides">MLWS</abbr> to achieve improved dispersion of the discharge of storm sewage, the following criterion may be adopted:</p>

<p>Achievement of the water quality standards of the Bathing Water Directive should be achieved in not less than 98.2% of the bathing season.</p>

<p>In such circumstances, the water and sewerage company should consider any offshore shellfish waters in their planning and modelling.</p>

<p>The impact criterion should only be used in those circumstances where extensive studies, including field exercises, can be undertaken and the regulatory authority with responsibility for auditing such information provided by the water and sewerage company can be reasonably satisfied with the validity of the assumptions made and the predictions produced.</p>

<h4 id="categories-of-receiving-water-aesthetic-amenity-and-value">7.2.6 Categories of receiving water aesthetic amenity and value</h4>

<p>The categories of amenity use outlined in section 7.3 should be used.</p>

<p>When assigning the amenity category, account should be taken of the affected receiving waters for a reasonable distance downstream as well as those in the immediate vicinity of the discharge.</p>

<h3 id="categories-of-receiving-water-aesthetic-amenity-and-value-1">7.3 Categories of receiving water aesthetic amenity and value</h3>

<p>Below are the categories used to describe the aesthetic amenity and value of receiving waters with examples of criteria used to define its amenity and value.</p>

<h4 id="high-amenity">7.3.1 High amenity</h4>

<p>Influences area where bathing and water contact sport (immersion) is regularly practised (such as wind-surfing, sports canoeing).</p>

<p>Receiving watercourse passes through formal public park.</p>

<p>Formal picnic site.</p>

<p>Designated shellfish waters.</p>

<p>Designated bathing waters.</p>

<p>Waters designated under the Conservation of Habitats and Species Regulations 2017 as special areas of conservation (<abbr title="special areas of conservation">SACs</abbr>).</p>

<p>Sites designated under the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands of International Importance especially as Waterfowl Habitat.</p>

<h4 id="moderate-amenity">7.3.2 Moderate amenity</h4>

<p>Boating on receiving water.</p>

<p>Popular footpath adjacent to watercourse.</p>

<p>Watercourse passes through housing development or frequently used town centre area (such as a bridge, pedestrian area, or shopping area).</p>

<p>Recreation and contact sport (non-immersion) areas.</p>

<p>It is linked through substantiated reasons for failure of Water Framework Directive water body status classification being less than good.</p>

<h4 id="low-amenity">7.3.3 Low amenity</h4>

<p>Basic amenity use only.</p>

<p>Casual riverside access on a limited or infrequent basis, such as a road bridge in a rural area, footpath adjacent to watercourse.</p>

<h4 id="non-amenity">7.3.4 Non-amenity</h4>

<p>Seldom or never used for amenity purposes.</p>

<p>Remote or inaccessible area.</p>
